results.text: What is taqwah? I want to know about this virtue in Islam.

base.reply:
Dear friend,

Taqwá is God-consciousness: a reverent awareness of God that guards a person from wrong. A note on the Arabic, which comes from me and not from a text: the word comes from the root *w-q-y*, "to guard, to shield." In that sense the *muttaqí* is one who keeps a protective watchfulness over themselves, and the word is often translated "piety" or "fear of God."

**In the Quran.** Rodwell's translation, in Sura II, rejects empty gesture: ["There is no piety in entering your houses at the back, but piety consists in the fear of God."](https://oceanlibrary.com/sura-ii-the-cow_muhammad/?paraId=para_116&selectionString=sura_ii_the_cow_quran_ocean_en-bl8f.0~sura_ii_the_cow_quran_ocean_en-bl8f.227) — [*The Quran (Rodwell)*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=214304). Sura IV opens with the call ["O MEN! fear your Lord, who hath created you of one man"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sura-iv-women_muhammad/?paraId=para_3&selectionString=sura_4_c_narration_ocean_en-blh1.0~sura_4_c_narration_ocean_en-blh1.221), which places taqwá at the root of our shared humanity. Sura 49:13 gives it the highest rank: the most honourable in God's sight is the believer who has taqwá. In the rendering quoted by Ibn Kathir, the *muttaqún* are those ["who fear Allah much, abstain from all kinds of sins and evil deeds which He has forbidden"](https://oceanlibrary.com/stories-of-the-prophets_imam-ibn-kathir/?paraId=para_2068&selectionString=al_anbiya_islam_ocean_en-bl1nu.0~al_anbiya_islam_ocean_en-bl1nu.405) and also love Allah much, doing the good He has ordained — [*Stories of the Prophets*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21076). So fear and love go together here.

**Inward, not for show.** Imam 'Ali says, ["By piety, the deeds are purified."](https://oceanlibrary.com/2500-adages-of-imam-ali/?paraId=para_633&selectionString=adages_islam_ocean_en-blk3.0~adages_islam_ocean_en-blk3.28) — [*2500 Adages of Imam Ali*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=945930). Saadi, in the [*Bustan*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21086), says the same about outward show: ["He whose heart is good and makes no outward show of piety is better than one of outward sanctity whose heart is false."](https://oceanlibrary.com/bustan-of-saadi/?paraId=para_461&selectionString=the_bustan_of_sadi_islam_ocean_en-blfi.0~the_bustan_of_sadi_islam_ocean_en-blfi.96)

**Stages, in the classical tradition.** Al-Ghazzálí, in [*Revival of Religious Learnings*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21042), describes fear in degrees. The lowest keeps a person from the unlawful. When fear is greater and keeps one from doubtful things, he writes, ["The meaning of Taqwa is to give up doubtful things and to act on things of sure faith."](https://oceanlibrary.com/revival-of-religious-learnings-vol-4_imam-ghazzali) Beyond that lies a state in which a person does not ["pass a minute without remembrance of God"](https://oceanlibrary.com/revival-of-religious-learnings-vol-4_imam-ghazzali), which he calls *sidq*, truthfulness. He also warns that the middle state of fear is best, since too much fear leads to despair and prevents action.

**In the Bahá'í Writings.** Here the nearest term is "fear of God." Bahá'u'lláh writes:

> We have admonished Our loved ones to fear God, a fear which is the fountainhead of all goodly deeds and virtues. It is the commander of the hosts of justice in the city of Bahá.
> — [*Fountain of Wisdom*](https://oceanlibrary.com/fountain-of-wisdom_bahaullah/?paraId=para_321&selectionString=tablets_of_baha_u_llah_revealed_after_the_kitab_i_73dc612de775bf9a04f878e400a2ce69-blby.0~tablets_of_baha_u_llah_revealed_after_the_kitab_i_73dc612de775bf9a04f878e400a2ce69-blby.307)

In the [*Gleanings*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20783) the human heart's ["raiment is the fear of God, and its perfection steadfastness in His Faith"](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_869&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_qv.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_qv.405). In the [*Epistle to the Son of the Wolf*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20780) he says ["The fear of God hath ever been the prime factor in the education of His creatures."](https://oceanlibrary.com/epistle-to-the-son-of-the-wolf_bahaullah/?paraId=para_57&selectionString=epistle_to_the_son_of_the_wolf_bahai_en-bl4b.0~epistle_to_the_son_of_the_wolf_bahai_en-bl4b.397) He also calls it ["a sure defence and a safe stronghold for all the peoples of the world" ([Epistle to the Son of the Wolf](https://oceanlibrary.com/epistle-to-the-son-of-the-wolf_bahaullah/?paraId=para_58&selectionString=epistle_to_the_son_of_the_wolf_bahai_en-bl4c.0~epistle_to_the_son_of_the_wolf_bahai_en-bl4c.611))](https://oceanlibrary.com/epistle-to-the-son-of-the-wolf_bahaullah/?paraId=para_58&selectionString=epistle_to_the_son_of_the_wolf_bahai_en-bl4c.611), and ties it to the human sense of shame, a faculty that guards against what is unworthy but, he says, is found in only a few.

It seems to me, and this is my reading, that the word "guard" in the Arabic root and Bahá'u'lláh's images of defence and stronghold are close companions. In both, taqwá protects a person from within.

If you would like to go further, read the opening of Sura II alongside the passage on fear of God in the *Epistle to the Son of the Wolf*. Notice how the Quran addresses taqwá to the individual conscience, and how Bahá'u'lláh follows it outward to kings, spiritual leaders and the preservation of mankind. It would be interesting to see what you find in that movement from private piety to the order of society.

With warm wishes,
Anís

claude-haiku-5-5.reply:
Taqwá is God-consciousness: a fear of God that guards a person from wrong. The Quran uses it as the measure of a good life. In Sura II, *The Cow*, the verse says that ["piety consists in the fear of God"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sura-ii-the-cow_muhammad/?paraId=para_116&selectionString=sura_ii_the_cow_quran_ocean_en-bl8f.0~sura_ii_the_cow_quran_ocean_en-bl8f.227) — [*The Quran*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=214150) (Rodwell).

**The word and its root.** Taqwá comes from a root meaning to guard or shield, so the word carries the sense of a protecting awareness. Those who have it are the *muttaqún*. Ibn Kathir's [*Stories of the Prophets*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21076) quotes Sura 49:13 and glosses the *muttaqún* as those who fear Allah much, abstain from what He has forbidden, and love Him much by doing what He has ordained. In that gloss, fear and love are held together, and the person who has taqwá is ["the most honorable of you in the Sight of Allah"](https://oceanlibrary.com/stories-of-the-prophets_imam-ibn-kathir/?paraId=para_2068&selectionString=al_anbiya_islam_ocean_en-bl1nu.0~al_anbiya_islam_ocean_en-bl1nu.405) — *Stories of the Prophets*.

**Inward reality, not outward gesture.** The Quran's verse on the new moons says there is ["no piety in entering your houses at the back"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sura-ii-the-cow_muhammad/?paraId=para_116&selectionString=sura_ii_the_cow_quran_ocean_en-bl8f.0~sura_ii_the_cow_quran_ocean_en-bl8f.227) — *The Quran* (Rodwell). The custom of entering houses by the back is set aside, and the piety that matters is the inner fear of God. Saadi makes the same point in [*The Bustan*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21086): ["He whose heart is good and makes no outward show of piety"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bustan-of-saadi/?paraId=para_461&selectionString=the_bustan_of_sadi_islam_ocean_en-blfi.0~the_bustan_of_sadi_islam_ocean_en-blfi.96) is better than one with false outward sanctity. Imam 'Ali's adage puts the same idea in a line: ["By piety, the deeds are purified."](https://oceanlibrary.com/2500-adages-of-imam-ali/?paraId=para_633&selectionString=adages_islam_ocean_en-blk3.0~adages_islam_ocean_en-blk3.28) — [*2500 Adages of Imam Ali*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=945930).

**Stages of fear.** Al-Ghazzálí's [*Revival of Religious Learnings*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21042) is a classical scholar's commentary, not scripture. He describes taqwá as growing in stages. The lowest fear keeps a person from what is unlawful. When fear is strong enough to keep a person from doubtful things too, [it is called Taqwa](https://oceanlibrary.com/revival-of-religious-learnings-vol-4_imam-ghazzali/?paraId=para_427&selectionString=the_revival_of_religious_learning_vol4_islam_ocean50a36bcc2251e1182f42f2dfde95a466-bl2k6.0~the_revival_of_religious_learning_vol4_islam_ocean50a36bcc2251e1182f42f2dfde95a466-bl2k6.1035) — *Revival of Religious Learnings*, Vol. IV. Its meaning, he writes, is to give up doubtful things and act on what is of sure faith. At its height, he describes a person who does not let a minute pass without remembrance of God, which he calls a further stage. He also holds that the middle state of fear is best, since too much fear [leads to despair](https://oceanlibrary.com/revival-of-religious-learnings-vol-4_imam-ghazzali) — *Revival of Religious Learnings*, Vol. IV.

**The Bahá'í Writings.** Bahá'u'lláh's Tablets call the fear of God ["a fear which is the fountainhead of all goodly deeds and virtues"](https://oceanlibrary.com/fountain-of-wisdom_bahaullah/?paraId=para_321&selectionString=tablets_of_baha_u_llah_revealed_after_the_kitab_i_73dc612de775bf9a04f878e400a2ce69-blby.0~tablets_of_baha_u_llah_revealed_after_the_kitab_i_73dc612de775bf9a04f878e400a2ce69-blby.307) — [*Fountain of Wisdom: Tablets of Bahá'u'lláh*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20781). In the [*Gleanings*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20783), fear is the heart's raiment: ["Its raiment is the fear of God"](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_869&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_qv.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_qv.405) — *Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá'u'lláh*.

**Moving from private piety to social order.** This is where the Epistle to the Son of the Wolf is most useful. Bahá'u'lláh writes that ["The fear of God hath ever been the prime factor in the education of His creatures"](https://oceanlibrary.com/epistle-to-the-son-of-the-wolf_bahaullah/?paraId=para_57&selectionString=epistle_to_the_son_of_the_wolf_bahai_en-bl4b.0~epistle_to_the_son_of_the_wolf_bahai_en-bl4b.397) — *Epistle to the Son of the Wolf*. In a related passage in the same Epistle, He says that ["The fear of God hath ever been a sure defence"](https://oceanlibrary.com/epistle-to-the-son-of-the-wolf_bahaullah/?paraId=para_58&selectionString=epistle_to_the_son_of_the_wolf_bahai_en-bl4c.0~epistle_to_the_son_of_the_wolf_bahai_en-bl4c.611) — *Epistle to the Son of the Wolf*, and that it is "the chief cause of the protection of mankind." He also links it to a faculty in man, the sense of shame, which guards against what is unworthy, and He notes that this faculty is found in only a few. For that reason He calls on kings and spiritual leaders to hold fast to religion, so that the fear of God is instilled in all others.

I read this as the shift that matters. In the Epistle, the same guarding fear becomes a public instrument, something rulers and teachers must cultivate to protect humanity. I'm reading "fear of God" in the Writings as the closest English match to taqwá; the Writings themselves do not use that comparison.

What would you make of the difference between a fear that guards a single heart and a fear that guards a whole society?

gemini-3.1-flash-lite.reply:
Hello. It is a pleasure to explore this with you. *Taqwá* is a rich, multi-layered concept, and looking at how it is understood in the Islamic tradition alongside the Bahá’í Writings reveals a beautiful continuity in how spiritual principles are meant to shape a human life.

**The core of taqwá**
At its heart, *taqwá* is often translated as "piety" or "God-consciousness." It is the inward state of being mindful of God, which naturally guards a person against actions that are unworthy. The Quran emphasizes that this is not a matter of outward ritual or gesture, but a condition of the heart: "There is no piety in entering your houses at the back, but piety consists in the fear of God" ([The Quran (Rodwell), Sura II. The Cow](https://oceanlibrary.com/sura-ii-the-cow_muhammad/?paraId=para_116&selectionString=sura_ii_the_cow_quran_ocean_en-bl8f.0~sura_ii_the_cow_quran_ocean_en-bl8f.227)) (Sura II:189). It is the "sure defence" that protects the soul from its own lower impulses.

**Inward reality and outward fruit**
The classical tradition often distinguishes between the outward appearance of holiness and the inward reality. As Saadi observed, "He whose heart is good and makes no outward show of piety is better than one of outward sanctity whose heart is false" ([The Bustan of Saadi](https://oceanlibrary.com/bustan-of-saadi/?paraId=para_461&selectionString=the_bustan_of_sadi_islam_ocean_en-blfi.0~the_bustan_of_sadi_islam_ocean_en-blfi.96)) (The Bustan of Saadi). Imam 'Ali similarly noted the transformative power of this virtue, stating, "By piety, the deeds are purified" ([2500 Adages of Imam Ali](https://oceanlibrary.com/2500-adages-of-imam-ali/?paraId=para_633&selectionString=adages_islam_ocean_en-blk3.0~adages_islam_ocean_en-blk3.28)) (2500 Adages of Imam Ali).

Al-Ghazzálí, in his [*Revival of Religious Learnings*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21042), describes *taqwá* as a graded journey. He suggests that while the beginning of fear is simply abstaining from the unlawful, *taqwá* matures into a state where one avoids even the "doubtful" things, eventually leading to a life of simplicity and constant remembrance of God.

**The Bahá’í perspective**
In the Bahá’í Writings, this same principle—often rendered as the "fear of God"—is described as the foundation of both individual virtue and social order. Bahá’u’lláh writes:

> "The first word which the Abhá Pen hath revealed and inscribed on the first leaf of Paradise is this: 'Verily I say: The fear of God hath ever been a sure defence and a safe stronghold for all the peoples of the world. It is the chief cause of the protection of mankind, and the supreme instrument for its preservation.'" (Epistle to the Son of the Wolf)

He also links this inward state to a "sense of shame" that acts as an internal guardian against the unseemly. In the [*Gleanings*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20783), He describes the soul’s journey.

```bilingual
رِدَاؤُهَا تَقْوَى اللهِ وَكَمَالُهَا الاسْتِقَامَةُ فِي أَمْرِهِ
Its raiment is the fear of God, and its perfection steadfastness in His Faith. <sup>1</sup>
```
<sup>1</sup> Authorized translation by Shoghi Effendi, [*Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20783)

While the Quranic *taqwá* and the Bahá’í "fear of God" share this root of mindful, protective reverence, Bahá’u’lláh explicitly moves this virtue from the realm of private piety into the public sphere. He calls it "the commander of the hosts of justice in the city of Bahá" ([Fountain of Wisdom : Tablets of Bahá’u’lláh](https://oceanlibrary.com/fountain-of-wisdom_bahaullah/?paraId=para_321&selectionString=tablets_of_baha_u_llah_revealed_after_the_kitab_i_73dc612de775bf9a04f878e400a2ce69-blby.0~tablets_of_baha_u_llah_revealed_after_the_kitab_i_73dc612de775bf9a04f878e400a2ce69-blby.307)) (Tablets of Bahá’u’lláh), suggesting that when this consciousness is instilled in a society, it becomes the primary factor in the education and protection of all people.

It is fascinating to see how a concept that begins as a personal guard against sin evolves into the very "instrument for the preservation" of human civilization. I wonder, as you look at these texts, how you see the relationship between that private "sense of shame" and the "hosts of justice" that Bahá’u’lláh describes?

gemini-3.5-flash-lite.reply:
Dear friend,

Taqwá is fundamentally God-consciousness and the inward vigilance that guards a person from wrong. In the Quran, it is closely tied to the very essence of righteousness, as seen when it declares that ["There is no piety in entering your houses at the back, but piety consists in the fear of God"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sura-ii-the-cow_muhammad/?paraId=para_116&selectionString=sura_ii_the_cow_quran_ocean_en-bl8f.0~sura_ii_the_cow_quran_ocean_en-bl8f.227) — [*The Quran (Rodwell)*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=214304) — reminding believers that ritual gesture alone does not constitute true devotion. Instead, the Quran repeatedly calls upon humanity to ["fear your Lord, who hath created you of one man"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sura-iv-women_muhammad/?paraId=para_3&selectionString=sura_4_c_narration_ocean_en-blh1.0~sura_4_c_narration_ocean_en-blh1.221) — *The Quran (Rodwell)*.

In the classical Islamic tradition, scholars like al-Ghazzálí outlined graded stages of this virtue. In his [*Revival of Religious Learnings*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21042), he explains that while the lowest form of fear keeps one from the unlawful, taqwá proper emerges when ["the proportion of fear is excessive and it keeps one away from doubtful things"](https://oceanlibrary.com/revival-of-religious-learnings-vol-4_imam-ghazzali/?paraId=para_427&selectionString=the_revival_of_religious_learning_vol4_islam_ocean50a36bcc2251e1182f42f2dfde95a466-bl2k6.0~the_revival_of_religious_learning_vol4_islam_ocean50a36bcc2251e1182f42f2dfde95a466-bl2k6.1035) — [*Revival of Religious Learnings Vol-IV*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21045). At its height, this state leads a person to simplicity and detachment, ["not to pass a minute without remembrance of God"](https://oceanlibrary.com/revival-of-religious-learnings-vol-4_imam-ghazzali). Al-Ghazzálí also notes that a moderate, balanced state of fear is best, as ["too much fear leads to despair and prevent actions"](https://oceanlibrary.com/revival-of-religious-learnings-vol-4_imam-ghazzali).

This inner reality shapes outward action. As Imam 'Ali concisely observes, ["By piety, the deeds are purified"](https://oceanlibrary.com/2500-adages-of-imam-ali/?paraId=para_633&selectionString=adages_islam_ocean_en-blk3.0~adages_islam_ocean_en-blk3.28) — [*2500 Adages of Imam Ali*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=945930). Similarly, the poet Sa'adi emphasizes the primacy of the inner state over mere appearances, writing that ["He whose heart is good and makes no outward show of piety is better than one of outward sanctity whose heart is false"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bustan-of-saadi/?paraId=para_461&selectionString=the_bustan_of_sadi_islam_ocean_en-blfi.0~the_bustan_of_sadi_islam_ocean_en-blfi.96) — [*The Bustan of Saadi*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21086).

In the Bahá'í Writings, this same virtue—rendered in Persian as *خشية الله* (the fear of God)—is described by Bahá'u'lláh as ["the fountainhead of all goodly deeds and virtues"](https://oceanlibrary.com/fountain-of-wisdom_bahaullah/?paraId=para_321&selectionString=tablets_of_baha_u_llah_revealed_after_the_kitab_i_73dc612de775bf9a04f878e400a2ce69-blby.0~tablets_of_baha_u_llah_revealed_after_the_kitab_i_73dc612de775bf9a04f878e400a2ce69-blby.307) — [*Fountain of Wisdom : Tablets of Bahá’u’lláh*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20781). In the [*Gleanings*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20783), He portrays spiritual perfection using vivid imagery, stating that the human heart's ["raiment is the fear of God, and its perfection steadfastness in His Faith"](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_869&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_qv.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_qv.405) — [*Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20783). Furthermore, in the *Epistle to the Son of the Wolf*, Bahá'u'lláh links this inner reverence directly to social order, noting that it ["hath ever been a sure defence and a safe stronghold for all the peoples of the world"](https://oceanlibrary.com/epistle-to-the-son-of-the-wolf_bahaullah/?paraId=para_58&selectionString=epistle_to_the_son_of_the_wolf_bahai_en-bl4c.0~epistle_to_the_son_of_the_wolf_bahai_en-bl4c.611) — *Epistle to the Son of the Wolf*, serving alongside humanity's innate sense of shame to guard against the unworthy.

Would you like to explore how Bahá'u'lláh moves this concept from a matter of private personal piety into the very foundation of social and political order in His letters to the leaders of the world?

Warmly,
Anís

results.text: Show me the Arabic original of this passage: 'Ask ye, therefore, of them that have the custody of the Scriptures, if ye know it not.'

base.reply:
Dear friend,

In the Persian text of the [*Kitáb-i-Íqán*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=28653), Bahá'u'lláh sets the Arabic verse inside His Persian prose, just after He says that everyone should bring the difficult questions of God's Faith to "the illumined in heart." The Arabic there reads: [فَاسْئَلُوا أَهْلَ الذِّكْرِ إِنْ كُنْتُمْ لَا تَعْلَمُونَ](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/core-tablets/bahaullah_kitab-i-iqan-the-book-of-certitude_fa#p57). Set beside Shoghi Effendi's English, clause by clause:

```bilingual
فَاسْئَلُوا أَهْلَ الذِّكْرِ
Ask ye, therefore, of them that have the custody of the Scriptures,<sup>1</sup>

إِنْ كُنْتُمْ لَا تَعْلَمُونَ
if ye know it not.<sup>1</sup>
```
<sup>1</sup> Authorized translation by Shoghi Effendi, [*The Kitáb-i-Íqán*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=28653)

The English closes the paragraph that begins ["Inasmuch as it hath been clearly shown that only those who are initiated into the divine mysteries"](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20810#p212) can comprehend the Bird of Heaven's melodies. The same paragraph is reproduced in the Research Department's [*Deepening*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/research-department-compilations/research-department_deepening) compilation.

**The Arabic is the Qur'anic verse.** The words are the Qur'an's own. It translates the Qur'anic Arabic as Bahá'u'lláh cites it.

**A note on the words** (from my knowledge of the language, not from a text):
- *Ahl* means "people of" or "folk of."
- [*Dhikr*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/papers/moojan-momen_dhikr-in-the-babi-and-bahai-religions) comes from the root ذ-ك-ر, meaning remembrance, mention or reminder. In Qur'anic usage it often points to scripture, and the "people of the Reminder" are often understood as those who hold the earlier revelation.
- That explains the English choice. That is why the English opens with "therefore."

In [*Gems*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20782) it points toward the custodians of earlier Scripture. Reading the two side by side, it seems to me that the verse carries more than one direction of meaning in His usage, though that is my own reading.

One thing you might pull on next: the verse also surfaces in the [*Íqán*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=28653)'s discussion of the 'ulamá of each age, where the Persian goes on to a Qur'anic citation about the People of the Book. Reading it there, beside this paragraph, shows how the same Arabic line works in two different settings.

With warm wishes for your reading,
Anís

base.reply:
Dear friend,

The Arabic has no word for "substance" in that clause.

```bilingual
هَلْ عَرَفْتُمْ لِمَ خَلَقْناكُمْ مِنْ تُرابٍ واحِدٍ؛
Know ye not why We created you all from the same dust?<sup>1</sup>

لِئَلاَّ يَفْتَخِرَ أَحَدٌ عَلى أَحَدٍ. That no one should exalt himself over the other.<sup>1</sup>

وَتَفَكَّرُوا فِي كُلِّ حِينٍ فِي خَلْقِ أَنْفُسِكُم؛
Ponder at all times in your hearts how ye were created.<sup>1</sup>

إِذاً يَنْبَغِي كَما خَلَقْناكُم مِنْ شَيْءٍ واحِدٍ
Since We have created you all from one same substance it is incumbent on you<sup>1</sup>

أَنْ تَكُونُوا كَنَفْسٍ واحِدَةٍ،
to be even as one soul,<sup>1</sup>
```

<sup>1</sup> Authorized translation by Shoghi Effendi, [*The Hidden Words*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/core-tablets/bahaullah_the-hidden-words_fa)

**The two origin words.** The first sentence says تُرابٍ واحِدٍ, "one dust." The second says شَيْءٍ واحِدٍ, literally "one thing." "Substance" is the translator's rendering of شيء. I read this as English reaching for the sense of a shared stuff, though the Arabic itself is plainer.

**Where "substance" or "essence" really lives.** The word that carries that sense is جوهر (jawhar), and it appears in the same verse, at the end: جَواهِرُ التَّجْرِيدِ, "the essence of detachment." It attaches to what our lives should show, not to where we come from. Shoghi Effendi renders جوهر as "essence" 29 times. Elsewhere it appears in:

- the Tablet of the Holy Mariner: ["created her out of the essence of love"](https://ctai.info/models/tablet-of-the-holy-mariner/54/);
- the Arabic Hidden Words: ["This is of the essence of My command"](https://ctai.info/models/the-hidden-words/17/);
- the Persian Hidden Words, in the address "O Essence of Negligence" ([link](https://ctai.info/models/the-hidden-words/90/)).

**The same idea in Persian.** In the [*Tablet to Mánikchí Ṣáḥib*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/bahaullah_tablet-to-manikchi-sahib-lawh-i-manikchi) the Persian reads مردم را یکسان آفریده, the Creator created people "alike," and goes on to say that rank depends on exertion ([Persian text](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/core-tablets/bahaullah_tablet-to-manikchi-sahib_fa-4#p2)). The English in [*Gleanings*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20783) is ["The incomparable Creator hath created all men from one same substance"](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20783#p146). Here too, "substance" goes a step beyond the Persian "alike."

**Dust elsewhere.** تراب (turáb) is rendered "dust" 18 times and "clay" twice. It recurs in the Persian Hidden Words: ["I have created all things from dust, and to dust will I return them again"](https://ctai.info/models/the-hidden-words/125/), and the address ["O Children of Dust"](https://ctai.info/models/the-hidden-words/126/). In both, dust is a ground for humility and generosity, not a technical term for matter.

So the idea of one origin recurs, but the vocabulary shifts: "dust," "one thing," "alike." The word "substance" is how the English draws them together.

If you would like to pull a thread, a word study of شيء (shay') across the Writings would show whether "substance" is ever its rendering, or whether it is mostly "things" and "creation," as it appears to be.

With warmth,
Anís

The Arabic word here is شيء واحد, literally "one same thing." *Shay'* means "thing" in ordinary use, and the English "substance" is the translator's rendering of it. This matters because the Arabic of the verse's first sentence speaks of تُرابٍ واحِدٍ, "one dust," and the English turns that into "the same dust." So the English makes two different words sound like one idea. I read the translator's choice as an effort to say something about the common stuff of humanity, but the Arabic itself says "thing," not "substance."

**The word that means "essence"**

The Arabic word that does carry the sense of "substance" or "essence" is جوهر, *jawhar*. Its root is ج و هـ, and classical Arabic used it for the essential nature of a thing. In this very passage it appears, but attached to detachment: جَواهِرُ التَّجْرِيدِ, "the essence of detachment." It is not attached to human origin.

That is a striking use, since it addresses the heedless as the "essence" of heedlessness.

Success or failure, gain or loss, must, therefore, depend upon man's own exertions." The English answers a question about "the sayings of the leaders of past religions," which matches the Persian's reference to the "گفته‌های آیین‌داران گذشته." I read this as the same passage in two languages. Once again, "substance" goes beyond the Persian "alike."

The Arabic word for dust is تراب, *turáb*. I have created all things from dust, and to dust will I return them again." Note that the Arabic speaks of *kull*, "all," rather than "man." In the *Hidden Words* numbered 49 the address "ای پسران تراب", "O Children of Dust," opens a counsel to the rich about the poor.

That would show whether the translators reached for "substance" as a considered choice or only here.

With warm regards,

base.reply:
Dear friend,

That line comes from Bahá'u'lláh's [*Tablet of the Holy Mariner*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=28677) (Lawh-i-Malláhu'l-Quds), and it also appears in [*Bahá'í Prayers*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahaullah/compilation-bahai_bahai-prayers). Here it is beside its Arabic:

```bilingual
ثمّ اركب عليها هياكل الرّوح باسم اللّه العليّ الأعلى
And let the angelic spirits enter, in the Name of God, the Most High.<sup>1</sup>

فسبحان ربّي الأبهى
Glorified be my Lord, the All-Glorious!<sup>1</sup>
```
<sup>1</sup> Published English translation, *Bahá'í Prayers*

**Its place in the tablet.** The line is one step in a voyage. The Arabic opens by addressing the "Mariner of holiness" (ملّاح القدس). He is told to bring the ark of eternity (سفينة البقاء) into the assembly on high, then to hold it fast on the sea of pre-eternity. Then comes your line, the boarding. After that he is told to let go the ship's reins so that it sails, in the English of the tablet, ["that it may sail upon the ocean of glory"](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_lawh_mallah_quds) — *Tablet of the Holy Mariner*. The purpose is given in the next verse: ["Haply the dwellers therein may attain the retreats of nearness in the everlasting realm."](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_lawh_mallah_quds) — *Tablet of the Holy Mariner*. Every step ends with the same refrain, "Glorified be my Lord, the All-Glorious!" ([Bahá’í Prayers](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-prayers/?paraId=para_837&selectionString=baha_i_prayers_bahai_ocean_en-bl1bc.0~baha_i_prayers_bahai_ocean_en-bl1bc.90))

**What the phrase means.** The Arabic words are *hayákil ar-rúḥ*. My own reading of the language is that اركب means "mount" or "board", so the English "enter" is a free rendering. هياكل is the plural of هيكل, which is literally a temple, frame or bodily form. "Angelic spirits" is a translator's interpretation of that phrase. It is a reasonable one, but not the only one.

**The same word elsewhere in the tablet.** The word returns later in the tablet, and the renderings differ:

- Of the arrival at the holy shore, the CTAI rendering says ["Wherein the embodiments of His Cause cleansed themselves of self and passion"](https://ctai.info/models/tablet-of-the-holy-mariner/9/) — *Tablet of the Holy Mariner*. Here هياكل is "embodiments".
- Of the shaking of the world, it says ["All beings were shaken in their mortal graves"](https://ctai.info/models/tablet-of-the-holy-mariner/29/) — *Tablet of the Holy Mariner*. Here هياكل is "beings".

Read together, the passengers come aboard as "forms of the spirit". On the far shore these same forms put off self and passion. I read this as a picture of souls becoming vessels of the spirit and then being stripped of what binds them. That is my own reading, not a stated interpretation. The tablet keeps the image of the ship and its crew throughout, which is what holds the sequence together.

A thread to pull: read the whole tablet once through, and at each appearance of هياكل ask whether "angelic spirits", "temples of the spirit", "embodiments" or "beings" best fits that moment. You may find the word means something slightly different in the boarding than at the shore.

With warmth,
Anís

Dear friend,

The line comes from Bahá'u'lláh's [*Tablet of the Holy Mariner*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=28677) (Lawh-i-Malláhu'l-Quds). The English line, "And let the angelic spirits enter, in the Name of God, the Most High," appears in the [*Bahá'í Prayers*](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-prayers/?paraId=para_837&selectionString=baha_i_prayers_bahai_ocean_en-bl1bc.0~baha_i_prayers_bahai_ocean_en-bl1bc.90) and in the [English text of the tablet](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_lawh_mallah_quds). The passages I found don't name the translator of that English, so I can't say more about who rendered it. Taherzadeh also quotes the same English line in [*Revelation*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20986), where it appears on page 231.

Note that the English verb is "enter," while the Arabic is "اركب," to mount or board. The English also turns هياكل الرّوح, literally "temples of the spirit," into "angelic spirits." That is a translator's choice, and the Arabic itself names no angels.

**What the line does in its setting**

The line is one step in a sequence, and the tablet is a voyage told as a series of commands. Only after that comes the release: "Unmoor it, then, that it may sail upon the ocean of glory," ([Tablet of the Holy Mariner (Lawh-i-Malláhu'l-Quds)](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_lawh_mallah_quds)) and so that the dwellers "may attain the retreats of nearness in the everlasting realm." Each step closes with the refrain "Glorified be my Lord, the All-Glorious!" ([Bahá’í Prayers](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-prayers/?paraId=para_837&selectionString=baha_i_prayers_bahai_ocean_en-bl1bc.0~baha_i_prayers_bahai_ocean_en-bl1bc.90)) (فسبحان ربّي الأبهى).

**The same word later in the tablet**

Later verses use هياكل for the passengers themselves.

So in this one tablet, هياكل appears in three renderings: "temples of the spirit" for what boards the ship, "embodiments of His Cause" for the passengers who cast off self, and "beings" for the existence shaken at the end.

**My reading**

It seems to me that the passengers are the ones who become هياكل, through the casting off of self and passion. If the boarding phrase meant angelic beings, the tablet would be describing a crew of angels who then shed self, which sits oddly with the rest of the image. "Temples of the spirit" or "embodiments of the spirit" keeps the sense of souls made fit to carry the spirit, as the later verses suggest. The heavenly host mentioned earlier gives "angelic" some support, so the choice is not clear-cut. I hold this as my own reading, not as the tablet's stated meaning.

Read the boarding line again in the sequence, then look at the CTAI renderings of the two later lines, and see which rendering of هياكل you think fits the crew and the passengers best.

With warm regards,
Anís

results.text: What do end times prophecies say about universal liberation?

base.reply:
Dear friend,

The word "liberation" appears less often in these texts than the thing itself: the lifting of oppression and the coming of justice and unity.

**The older promise.** Isaiah, speaking of Egypt, says the people ["shall cry unto the LORD because of the oppressors, and he shall send them a saviour, and a great one, and he shall deliver them"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kjv-book-of-isaiah/?paraId=para_331&selectionString=isaiah-ot_en_bw.0~isaiah-ot_en_bw.180) — [*Isaiah*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21231). In the Shi'i tradition gathered by Majlisi, Adam is shown a luminous figure, and God says that through him ["I will take away the chains of oppressors from the necks of My servants"](https://oceanlibrary.com/hayat-al-qulub-vol2_muhammad-majlisi/?paraId=para_5829&selectionString=hayat_al_qulub_vol_2_islam_ocean_en-bl4jh.0~hayat_al_qulub_vol_2_islam_ocean_en-bl4jh.485) and fill the earth with justice — [*Hayat al-Qulub*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21051). In both, oppression comes first and deliverance follows.

**Bahá'u'lláh.** In the [*Tablet on the Paradise of Justice*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/bahaullah_tablet-on-the-paradise-of-justice-lawh-i-ridvanul-adl) He says that the day is approaching when God will raise up manifestations of the name of justice, [“through whom We shall roll up the standard of oppression and unfurl the banner of justice between the heavens and the earth”](http://bahaiprovisionaltablets.blogspot.com/2018/06/lawh-i-ridvanul-adl-paradise-of-justice.html), so that God ["shall blot out every trace of injustice from the earth"](http://bahaiprovisionaltablets.blogspot.com/2018/06/lawh-i-ridvanul-adl-paradise-of-justice.html). In the [*Kitáb-i-Aqdas*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21307) He ties justice to His own suffering: ["because of His endurance of oppression, justice hath become manifest in aught else"](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_kitab_aqdas_parallel).

**'Abdu'l-Bahá's reading.** He says that all peoples were promised two successive Manifestations, through whom ["justice and righteousness will encompass the globe; hatred and enmity will disappear"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-sacred-writings/?paraId=para_1030&selectionString=baha_i_sacred_writings_en-blv5.0~baha_i_sacred_writings_en-blv5.1101) — [*Bahá'í Sacred Writings*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahaullah/compilation-bahai_bahai-sacred-writings). In [*Some Answered Questions*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20911), on the "Standard of God" raised among the nations, He describes the form this takes:

> Religious and sectarian antagonism, the hostility of races and peoples, and differences among nations will be eliminated. All men will adhere to one religion, will have one common faith, will be blended into one race and become a single people. All will dwell in one common fatherland, which is the planet itself.
> — [*Some Answered Questions*](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_219&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_94.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_94.817)

So the freedom described is from the divisions that breed oppression: race, creed and nation. He adds that ["universal peace is assured by Bahá'u'lláh as a fundamental accomplishment of the religion of God"](https://oceanlibrary.com/promulgation-of-universal-peace_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_2081&selectionString=promulgation_of_universal_peace_ocean_en_1oh.0~promulgation_of_universal_peace_ocean_en_1oh.263) — [*The Promulgation of Universal Peace*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20917). In [*Paris Talks*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20908) he says simply, ["Justice will come and reign upon the earth"](https://oceanlibrary.com/paris-talks_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_667&selectionString=abdu-l-baha-paris-talks_en_la.0~abdu-l-baha-paris-talks_en_la.79).

**Already begun?** He also reads the prophecies as under way. Of people from many religions who have entered the Cause, he says they ["all consort together with perfect love and fellowship"](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_218&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_93.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_93.479) and calls this one meaning of the wolf lying down with the lamb — *Some Answered Questions*.

**Shoghi Effendi's horizon.** He sees a culmination still ahead: ["the coming of age of the entire human race"](https://oceanlibrary.com/promised-day-is-come_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_340&selectionString=the_promised_day_is_come_bahai_ocean_en-blbk.0~the_promised_day_is_come_bahai_ocean_en-blbk.1120) will be proclaimed, the banner of the Most Great Peace hoisted, and a world civilization born — *The Promised Day Is Come*.

**Not painless.** As recalled by Breakwell, Hopper and Brittingham, 'Abdu'l-Bahá said that ["Before the universal peace is established there will be wars and a general overturning of society"](https://bahai-library.com/breakwell_hopper_brittingham). In my reading, these texts do not describe an automatic or bloodless arrival. The peace is promised, but through a turbulent passage.

**My own observation:** the sources keep returning to justice, the end of oppression and the oneness of humankind. If you quote them, I'd keep those words rather than substituting "liberation," which carries modern meanings the texts don't state.

A thread to pull: Nader Saiedi's article "From Oppression to Empowerment," in the *Journal of Bahá'í Studies*, is scholarly commentary on how Bahá'u'lláh Himself met oppression and what the Bahá'í approach to empowerment draws from it. It may help you ask how these promises bear on social liberation as people live it.

With warm wishes,
Anís

claude-haiku-5-5.reply:
Dear friend,

The promise you're asking about runs through several scriptures, and the Bahá'í Writings read it in a particular way. I'll start with the older texts, then show how Bahá'u'lláh and 'Abdu'l-Bahá apply it.

**The promise in the older scriptures.** Isaiah describes a people crying out "because of the oppressors," and the answer is that God will "send them a saviour, and a great one, and he shall deliver them" (["they shall cry unto the LORD because of the oppressors"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kjv-book-of-isaiah/?paraId=para_331&selectionString=isaiah-ot_en_bw.0~isaiah-ot_en_bw.180) — [*The Bible (KJV), Isaiah*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=912528)). A Shi'i tradition recorded by Muhammad Baqir Majlisi has the Most High say of a future servant: ["I will take away the chains of oppressors from the necks of My servants"](https://oceanlibrary.com/hayat-al-qulub-vol2_muhammad-majlisi/?paraId=para_5829&selectionString=hayat_al_qulub_vol_2_islam_ocean_en-bl4jh.0~hayat_al_qulub_vol_2_islam_ocean_en-bl4jh.485) — [*Hayat Al-Qulub Vol.2*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21051). These are comparative witnesses. They show a shared hope, and the Bahá'í Writings read it through their own framework.

**Bahá'u'lláh's application.** In the [*Tablet on the Paradise of Justice*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/bahaullah_tablet-on-the-paradise-of-justice-lawh-i-ridvanul-adl), Bahá'u'lláh speaks of manifestations through whom God will "roll up the standard of oppression and unfurl the banner of justice," and says that "God shall blot out every trace of injustice from the earth" ([link](http://bahaiprovisionaltablets.blogspot.com/2018/06/lawh-i-ridvanul-adl-paradise-of-justice.html)). In the [*Kitáb-i-Aqdas*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21307) He ties the manifestation of justice to His own suffering: ["because of His endurance of oppression, justice hath become manifest"](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_kitab_aqdas_parallel) — [*The Most Holy Book*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/bahaullah_the-most-holy-book-parallel-translation-of-the-kitab-i-aqdas). I read this as a claim that justice has come through endurance rather than through force.

**'Abdu'l-Bahá's description.** He says that through the twin Manifestations "the earth will become another earth," and that ["justice and righteousness will encompass the globe; hatred and enmity will disappear"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-sacred-writings/?paraId=para_1030&selectionString=baha_i_sacred_writings_en-blv5.0~baha_i_sacred_writings_en-blv5.1101) — [*Bahá'í Sacred Writings*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahaullah/compilation-bahai_bahai-sacred-writings). In the [*Paris Talks*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20908) the same hope appears in the line ["Justice will come and reign upon the earth"](https://oceanlibrary.com/paris-talks_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_667&selectionString=abdu-l-baha-paris-talks_en_la.0~abdu-l-baha-paris-talks_en_la.79) — *Paris Talks*.

**Unity as the form the promise takes.** The Writings speak more often of unity than of liberation as such. In [*Some Answered Questions*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20911) 'Abdu'l-Bahá describes a time when "religious and sectarian antagonism, the hostility of races and peoples, and differences among nations will be eliminated," and when "All will dwell in one common fatherland, which is the planet itself" ([link](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_219&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_94.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_94.817)). *The Promulgation of Universal Peace* states that ["Universal peace is assured by Bahá'u'lláh as a fundamental accomplishment of the religion of God"](https://oceanlibrary.com/promulgation-of-universal-peace_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_2081&selectionString=promulgation_of_universal_peace_ocean_en_1oh.0~promulgation_of_universal_peace_ocean_en_1oh.263) — *The Promulgation of Universal Peace*.

A pilgrim's record of 'Abdu'l-Bahá's utterances, taken down by Thomas Breakwell, Herbert Hopper and Isabella D. Brittingham, has Him say that ["all the inhabitants of the world will be gathered into one nation; universal peace will prevail; bloodshed and war will cease"](https://bahai-library.com/breakwell_hopper_brittingham). This is a recollection rather than a written text, so I'd hold it more loosely than the Tablets.

**The present and the process.** 'Abdu'l-Bahá points to signs already visible: ["Christians, Jews, Zoroastrians, Hindus, Buddhists, and Persians all consort together with perfect love and fellowship"](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_218&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_93.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_93.479) — *Some Answered Questions*. Shoghi Effendi reads the fulfilment as a process that unfolds over time. He writes that ["Then will a world civilization be born, flourish, and perpetuate"](https://oceanlibrary.com/promised-day-is-come_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_340&selectionString=the_promised_day_is_come_bahai_ocean_en-blbk.0~the_promised_day_is_come_bahai_ocean_en-blbk.1120) — *The Promised Day is Come*.

**A turbulent passage first.** The same pilgrim's record says that "Before the universal peace is established there will be wars and a general overturning of society." ([Utterances of Abdu'l-Baha to Thomas Breakwell, Herbert Hopper, and Isabella D. Brittingham](https://bahai-library.com/breakwell_hopper_brittingham)) So the peace is tied to a painful transition. It is not presented as automatic, and I'd be going beyond the texts to call it bloodless.

**A word on vocabulary.** The Writings speak of justice, the ending of oppression and the unity of mankind. "Liberation" is a useful word for our conversation, but when you quote them, the vocabulary of justice and unity keeps closer to their wording.

The thread I'd pull next is Nader Saiedi's article "From Oppression to Empowerment" in the *Journal of Bahá'í Studies*. It takes up Bahá'u'lláh's personal response to oppression and the Bahá'í approach to empowerment, which is where the prophetic promise meets the question of social liberation. It's commentary rather than scripture, but it's a good companion to the Tablets.

With warmth,
Anís

gemini-3.1-flash-lite.reply:
Dear friend,

It is a pleasure to explore these questions with you. The promise of an end-times liberation from oppression is a deep, recurring theme in the scriptures of the world, and the Bahá’í Writings speak to this by framing the transition not as a sudden, automatic utopia, but as a profound, often turbulent process of transformation.

In the traditions that the Bahá’í Writings treat as prophetic, the cry for deliverance is central. In [*Isaiah*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21231), the people call out "because of the oppressors" and are promised that God "shall send them a saviour, and a great one, and he shall deliver them" [](https://oceanlibrary.com/kjv-book-of-isaiah/?paraId=para_331&selectionString=isaiah-ot_en_bw.0~isaiah-ot_en_bw.180). Similarly, in Islamic tradition, there is the promise of a figure who will "take away the chains of oppressors from the necks of My servants" and "fill the earth with light, mercy and justice" after a period of tyranny [](https://oceanlibrary.com/hayat-al-qulub-vol2_muhammad-majlisi/?paraId=para_5829&selectionString=hayat_al_qulub_vol_2_islam_ocean_en-bl4jh.0~hayat_al_qulub_vol_2_islam_ocean_en-bl4jh.485).

Bahá’u’lláh applies these promises to His own Revelation, though He speaks primarily of the establishment of justice and the unity of humanity rather than using the term "liberation." He writes that the day is approaching when God will raise up manifestations of His name "through whom We shall roll up the standard of oppression and unfurl the banner of justice between the heavens and the earth" ([Tablet on the Paradise of Justice (Lawh-i-Ridván al-'Adl)](http://bahaiprovisionaltablets.blogspot.com/2018/06/lawh-i-ridvanul-adl-paradise-of-justice.html)). He also emphasizes that this justice is inextricably linked to the suffering of the Manifestation Himself:

> "Say, because of His endurance of oppression, justice hath become manifest in aught else; because of His acceptance of humility, the might of God hath shone forth amidst the worlds." [](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_kitab_aqdas_parallel)

‘Abdu’l-Bahá describes the fulfillment of these prophecies as a renewal of the world itself. He explains that through the twin Manifestations, "the earth will become another earth; all existence will be renewed; the contingent world will be clothed with the robe of a new life; justice and righteousness will encompass the globe" [](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-sacred-writings/?paraId=para_1030&selectionString=baha_i_sacred_writings_en-blv5.0~baha_i_sacred_writings_en-blv5.1101). He further notes that "Justice will come and reign upon the earth" [](https://oceanlibrary.com/paris-talks_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_667&selectionString=abdu-l-baha-paris-talks_en_la.0~abdu-l-baha-paris-talks_en_la.79).

This liberation takes the form of the unity of humanity. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá describes a future where "all nations and kindreds will be gathered together under the shadow of this Divine Banner" and "will become a single nation" [](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_219&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_94.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_94.817). He asserts that "universal peace is assured by Bahá’u’lláh as a fundamental accomplishment of the religion of God" [](https://oceanlibrary.com/promulgation-of-universal-peace_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_2081&selectionString=promulgation_of_universal_peace_ocean_en_1oh.0~promulgation_of_universal_peace_ocean_en_1oh.263).

However, the Writings also warn of a painful passage. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá observed that "before the universal peace is established there will be wars and a general overturning of society" [](https://bahai-library.com/breakwell_hopper_brittingham). Shoghi Effendi, in interpreting this process, speaks of the "coming of age of the entire human race" and the birth of a "world civilization" [](https://oceanlibrary.com/promised-day-is-come_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_340&selectionString=the_promised_day_is_come_bahai_ocean_en-blbk.0~the_promised_day_is_come_bahai_ocean_en-blbk.1120).

To see how these concepts are rendered in the original, consider this passage from the [*Kitáb-i-Aqdas*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21307).

```bilingual
قُلْ بِتَحَمُّلِهِ الظُّلْمَ ظَهَرَ الْعَدْلُ فِي كُلِّ الْأَشْيَاءِ
Say, because of His endurance of oppression, justice hath become manifest in aught else; <sup>1</sup>

وَبِقَبُولِهِ الذُّلَّ أَشْرَقَتْ عِزَّةُ اللهِ بَيْنَ الْعَالَمِينَ
because of His acceptance of humility, the might of God hath shone forth amidst the worlds. <sup>1</sup>
```
<sup>1</sup> [*The Most Holy Book: Parallel Translation of the Kitáb-i-Aqdas*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/bahaullah_the-most-holy-book-parallel-translation-of-the-kitab-i-aqdas)

If you wish to delve deeper into how these spiritual principles translate into the struggle for social empowerment, you might find Nader Saiedi’s [*From Oppression to Empowerment*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/papers/nader-saiedi_from-oppression-to-empowerment) a compelling thread to pull. It explores how the Bahá’í approach to these themes moves beyond mere theory into the realm of personal and collective response to the conditions of the world.

Warmly,

Anís

Hello friend,

The prophetic promise in older scriptures speaks plainly of deliverance from oppressors. In the Book of Isaiah, the people cry out "because of the oppressors," prompting God to send "a saviour, and a great one" to deliver them [1](https://oceanlibrary.com/kjv-book-of-isaiah/?paraId=para_331&selectionString=isaiah-ot_en_bw.0~isaiah-ot_en_bw.180). Islamic traditions likewise record descriptions of a future figure who will "take away the chains of oppressors from the necks of My servants" and fill the earth with justice after a time of tyranny [2](https://oceanlibrary.com/hayat-al-qulub-vol2_muhammad-majlisi/?paraId=para_5829&selectionString=hayat_al_qulub_vol_2_islam_ocean_en-bl4jh.0~hayat_al_qulub_vol_2_islam_ocean_en-bl4jh.485).

The Bahá’í Writings apply these promises directly to the current Revelation, framing the end-times liberation not as a sudden utopian break, but as the establishment of divine justice and the unification of the human race. Bahá’u’lláh writes that the day approaches when God will raise up those who will "roll up the standard of oppression and unfurl the banner of justice between the heavens and the earth" [3](http://bahaiprovisionaltablets.blogspot.com/2018/06/lawh-i-ridvanul-adl-paradise-of-justice.html). At the same time, He notes that "because of His endurance of oppression, justice hath become manifest in aught else" [11](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_kitab_aqdas_parallel).

‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains that the twin Manifestations will renew existence, ensuring that "justice and righteousness will encompass the globe; hatred and enmity will disappear; whatever is the cause of division among peoples, races, and nations will be obliterated" [10](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-sacred-writings/?paraId=para_1030&selectionString=baha_i_sacred_writings_en-blv5.0~baha_i_sacred_writings_en-blv5.1101). In His talks in Paris, He affirms simply that "Justice will come and reign upon the earth" [9](https://oceanlibrary.com/paris-talks_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_667&selectionString=abdu-l-baha-paris-talks_en_la.0~abdu-l-baha-paris-talks_en_la.79).

This liberation takes the specific form of human unity. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá details that religious and racial antagonisms will be eliminated, resulting in one common faith and "one common fatherland, which is the planet itself" ([Some Answered Questions](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_219&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_94.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_94.817)) 7. He states explicitly that "universal peace is assured by Bahá’u’lláh as a fundamental accomplishment of the religion of God" [4](https://oceanlibrary.com/promulgation-of-universal-peace_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_2081&selectionString=promulgation_of_universal_peace_ocean_en_1oh.0~promulgation_of_universal_peace_ocean_en_1oh.263). He notes that signs of this are already visible as diverse peoples consort together "as if they were father and son, mother and daughter, sister and brother" ([Some Answered Questions](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_218&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_93.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_93.479)) 6.

Shoghi Effendi similarly projects this process forward, writing of a time when the coming of age of humanity will be celebrated, "the banner of the Most Great Peace be hoisted," and a new world civilization born [8](https://oceanlibrary.com/promised-day-is-come_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_340&selectionString=the_promised_day_is_come_bahai_ocean_en-blbk.0~the_promised_day_is_come_bahai_ocean_en-blbk.1120).

Crucially, the texts do not picture this transition as automatic or bloodless. Pilgrim records of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s statements note that "before the universal peace is established there will be wars and a general overturning of society" [5](https://bahai-library.com/breakwell_hopper_brittingham). The vocabulary of the Writings centers primarily on justice, the ending of oppression, and organic unity rather than modern political terms of "liberation."

If you would like to explore how Bahá'u'lláh's own response to imprisonment and persecution shapes the Bahá'í approach to overcoming oppression, Nader Saiedi’s study [*From Oppression to Empowerment*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/papers/nader-saiedi_from-oppression-to-empowerment) offers a thoughtful look at that dynamic.

Warmly,
Anís

results.text: words of comfort when someone dies

base.reply:
Dear friend,

The most direct line comes from Bahá'u'lláh, in [*The Hidden Words*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/core-tablets/bahaullah_the-hidden-words_fa):

> ["I have made death a messenger of joy to thee. Wherefore dost thou grieve?"](https://oceanlibrary.com/hidden-words-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_104&selectionString=the-hidden-words-prod_en_5n.0~the-hidden-words-prod_en_5n.146) — *The Hidden Words*

It is short enough for a single card.

'Abdu'l-Bahá's tablets to the bereaved return to the same few images, of release and homecoming. To one mourning a brother he writes: ["That drop hath hastened to the limitless Ocean; that homeless bird hath winged its flight unto the sheltering nest of the Concourse on high."](https://oceanlibrary.com/light-of-the-world_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_443&selectionString=light_of_the_world_baha_i_ocean_en-blfe.0~light_of_the_world_baha_i_ocean_en-blfe.285) — [*Light of the World*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20906). To a father who has lost a son, he says the boy has left ["this narrow and gloomy world which is darkened by unlimited sorrow"](https://oceanlibrary.com/tablets-of-abdul-baha-abbas-vol-1-3/?paraId=para_334&selectionString=tablets_of_abdu_l_baha_abbas_v1_3_bahai_ocean_en-blb1.0~tablets_of_abdu_l_baha_abbas_v1_3_bahai_ocean_en-blb1.366) for a Kingdom that is spacious and illumined — [*Tablets of 'Abdu'l-Bahá 'Abbás*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20915). In another tablet he asks the mourner to hold to faith in a heavenly world and not to wail or weep, ["for agitation and mourning deeply affect his soul in the divine realm" ([Selections from the Writings of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-abdul-baha/?paraId=para_1065&selectionString=selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_112.0~selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_112.253))](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-abdul-baha/?paraId=para_1065&selectionString=selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_112.253) — [*Selections from the Writings of 'Abdu'l-Bahá*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20910).

Bahá'u'lláh's [*Tablet of Consolation*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/bahaullah_tablet-of-consolation-2) turns grief toward God: ["Trust in Him and immerse yourself in His praise."](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_hall_tablet_consolation) — [*Tablet of Consolation (Lawḥ-i ta'ziya)*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/bahaullah_tablet-of-consolation-2). The tablet then bids the reader be gladdened.

Shoghi Effendi's condolences, or those written on his behalf, follow the same pattern. After a young believer's death in Japan, the letter says ["Our sole comfort should be in this that he is at present in a higher spiritual realm"](https://bahai-library.com/alexander_history_bahai_japan&chapter=all) — [*History of the Bahá'í Faith in Japan 1914-1938*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/agnes-baldwin_history-of-the-bahai-faith-in-japan-1914-1938), by Alexander. They also add the act of prayer, because ["prayers for departed souls is the greatest help we can render them"](https://oceanlibrary.com/uncompiled-published-letters_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_1316&selectionString=published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl13c.0~published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl13c.208), the Master's assurance, as the letter recalls it — [*Uncompiled Published Letters*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20897). Duane Herrmann quotes the Guardian's own condolence for a departed believer in *'Abdu'l-Bahá Writes to Kansas City*: ["I will pray for her soul from the depths of my heart."](https://bahai-library.com/herrmann_abdul-baha_kansas_city)

This is my own reading, not a teaching: these writings console with images of release and reunion and with the promise of prayer, and they don't try to explain the death. A short note that names the loss, offers one of these images, and promises prayer would follow their pattern.

If you'd like a thread to pull, the whole *Tablet of Consolation* is the longer form of comfort. The Hidden Words line is the one most likely to fit a single letter.

With warmth,
Anís

gemini-3.1-flash-lite.reply:
Dear friend,

When we face the loss of someone dear, the Writings offer a perspective that shifts our gaze from the finality of the physical world to the continuity of the spirit. They do not ask us to ignore our sorrow, but rather to find a deeper, more enduring comfort in the reality of the soul’s journey.

Bahá’u’lláh speaks directly to the heart in [*The Hidden Words*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/core-tablets/bahaullah_the-hidden-words_fa), inviting us to see death not as an end, but as a transition:

> O Son of the Supreme!
> I have made death a messenger of joy to thee. Wherefore dost thou grieve? I made the light to shed on thee its splendor. Why dost thou veil thyself therefrom? [1](https://oceanlibrary.com/hidden-words-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_104&selectionString=the-hidden-words-prod_en_5n.0~the-hidden-words-prod_en_5n.146)

In His tablets of consolation, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá often uses the imagery of release. He describes the departed as having been freed from a "narrow and gloomy world" to soar toward a "Kingdom which is spacious, illumined, joyous and beautiful" [3](https://oceanlibrary.com/tablets-of-abdul-baha-abbas-vol-1-3/?paraId=para_334&selectionString=tablets_of_abdu_l_baha_abbas_v1_3_bahai_ocean_en-blb1.0~tablets_of_abdu_l_baha_abbas_v1_3_bahai_ocean_en-blb1.366). He compares the soul to a drop returning to the "limitless Ocean" or a bird finding its way to a "sheltering nest" [2](https://oceanlibrary.com/light-of-the-world_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_443&selectionString=light_of_the_world_baha_i_ocean_en-blfe.0~light_of_the_world_baha_i_ocean_en-blfe.285).

While these images provide a sense of peace, the Writings also offer a practical way to remain connected to those who have passed on. Shoghi Effendi often reminded the bereaved that prayer is the most meaningful gift we can offer. He noted that "prayers for departed souls is the greatest help we can render them" [6](https://oceanlibrary.com/uncompiled-published-letters_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_1316&selectionString=published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl13c.0~published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl13c.208). In his own letters of condolence, he frequently expressed that our "sole comfort should be in this that he is at present in a higher spiritual realm enjoying a blissful being far beyond our powers to appreciate" [7](https://bahai-library.com/alexander_history_bahai_japan&chapter=all).

When you are ready, you might find it helpful to read the [*Tablet of Consolation*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/bahaullah_tablet-of-consolation-2) (Lawḥ-i-Ṭa'ziya) in its entirety, as it beautifully frames the act of grieving as a way of turning toward God, who is the ultimate source of all solace [5](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_hall_tablet_consolation).

I hope these words bring a measure of quiet to your heart.

Warmly,

Anís

gemini-3.5-flash-lite.reply:
Hello, my friend.

When death touches someone we care for, the writings of the tradition offer comfort not by explaining the mechanics of loss, but by pointing toward release and renewal. They speak of the departed as having passed from a restricted state into a vast one—as Bahá’u’lláh writes in [*The Hidden Words*](https://oceanlibrary.com/hidden-words-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_104&selectionString=the-hidden-words-prod_en_5n.0~the-hidden-words-prod_en_5n.146): ["I have made death a messenger of joy to thee. Wherefore dost thou grieve?"](https://oceanlibrary.com/hidden-words-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_104&selectionString=the-hidden-words-prod_en_5n.0~the-hidden-words-prod_en_5n.146) [*The Hidden Words of Bahá’u’lláh*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20809) ([The Hidden Words of Bahá’u’lláh](https://oceanlibrary.com/hidden-words-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_104&selectionString=the-hidden-words-prod_en_5n.0~the-hidden-words-prod_en_5n.146)).

In letters of condolence, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá frequently used the image of a drop returning to the ocean or a bird freed from a narrow cage, urging those left behind to recognize that the one who has died has departed from [*this narrow and gloomy world which is darkened by unlimited sorrow, unto the Kingdom which is spacious, illumined, joyous and beautiful*](https://oceanlibrary.com/tablets-of-abdul-baha-abbas-vol-1-3/?paraId=para_334&selectionString=tablets_of_abdu_l_baha_abbas_v1_3_bahai_ocean_en-blb1.0~tablets_of_abdu_l_baha_abbas_v1_3_bahai_ocean_en-blb1.366) [*Tablets of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá ‘Abbás vol. 1-3*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20915) ([Tablets of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá ‘Abbás vol. 1-3](https://oceanlibrary.com/tablets-of-abdul-baha-abbas-vol-1-3/?paraId=para_334&selectionString=tablets_of_abdu_l_baha_abbas_v1_3_bahai_ocean_en-blb1.0~tablets_of_abdu_l_baha_abbas_v1_3_bahai_ocean_en-blb1.366)). At the same time, mourners are gently counseled against excessive outward grief, with ‘Abdu’l-Bahá noting that [*agitation and mourning deeply affect his soul in the divine realm*](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-abdul-baha/?paraId=para_1065&selectionString=selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_112.0~selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_112.253) [*Selections from the Writings of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20910) ([Selections from the Writings of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-abdul-baha/?paraId=para_1065&selectionString=selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_112.0~selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_112.253)).

The letters written on behalf of Shoghi Effendi follow this same pattern, reminding a bereaved friend that [*our sole comfort should be in this that he is at present in a higher spiritual realm enjoying a blissful being*](https://bahai-library.com/alexander_history_bahai_japan&chapter=all) [*History of the Bahá’í Faith in Japan 1914-1938*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/agnes-baldwin_history-of-the-bahai-faith-in-japan-1914-1938) ([History of the Bahá’í Faith in Japan 1914-1938](https://bahai-library.com/alexander_history_bahai_japan&chapter=all)), while actively offering the practical support of prayer, which is described as [*the greatest help we can render them*](https://oceanlibrary.com/uncompiled-published-letters_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_1316&selectionString=published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl13c.0~published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl13c.208) [*Uncompiled Published Letters*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20897) ([Uncompiled Published Letters](https://oceanlibrary.com/uncompiled-published-letters_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_1316&selectionString=published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl13c.0~published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl13c.208)).

Read the [*Tablet of Consolation*](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_hall_tablet_consolation) for the longer form of comfort, and [*The Hidden Words*](https://oceanlibrary.com/hidden-words-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_104&selectionString=the-hidden-words-prod_en_5n.0~the-hidden-words-prod_en_5n.146) for the single line most likely to fit a short note.

base.reply:
Dear friend,

The passages I found trace Iran's Bahá'í story through its sufferings and what came of them. Here are the threads they hold.

**The Báb's martyrdom.** In [*God Passes By*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21310), Shoghi Effendi records that the Báb's execution at Tabríz ["fell on the ninth of July 1850"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_129&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_6c.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_6c.1397), in the seventh year of His ministry. That evening the mangled bodies were carried to the edge of the moat outside the city gate, where sentinels were set to watch over them.

**The Síyáh-Chál.** Bahá'u'lláh was delivered into His enemies' hands and taken from Níyávarán to the Síyáh-Chál of Ṭihrán ["on foot and in chains, with bared head and bare feet"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_159&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en-blwk.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en-blwk.2405), exposed to the midsummer sun. Nabíl's [*The Dawn-Breakers*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21308) preserves what Bahá'u'lláh told of that prison. The companions of the Báb who were struck down in Ṭihrán that year were His fellow-prisoners, and [“We were all huddled together in one cell, our feet in stocks”](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_1875&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_1is.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_1is.1345).

**Expulsion from Persia.** The Sháh's edict amounted to an order for Bahá'u'lláh's immediate expulsion from Persian territory. Shoghi Effendi says it [“opens a new and glorious chapter in the history of the first Bahá’í century”](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_232&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_97.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_97.2019) and coincides with the start of a ministry of almost forty years. In this telling, the Faith's story did not end when its Founder left Iran.

**The 1903 pogroms.** In the summer of 1903 the community in Iran faced brutal campaigns in several cities, including Rasht, Isfahán and Yazd. The introduction to [*Treatise on Persecution of Bahá'ís in 1903*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/abdul-baha_treatise-on-persecution-of-bahais-in-1903#p7) says that when the persecutions peaked, 'Abdu'l-Bahá wrote a treatise outlining the events, the motives and actions of the chief persecutors, and the community's sufferings.

**Shoghi Effendi's response.** Writing in [*Bahá'í Administration*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20880) about later events in Persia, he spoke of ["burning indignation"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-administration_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_793&selectionString=baha_i_administration_selected_messages_1922_1932_3521e4ac6904cefdca84fce2627329c7-blug.335). He added that such happenings [“cannot but eventually contribute to the strengthening and purification of the Cause we steadfastly love and serve” ([Bahá’í Administration](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-administration_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_793&selectionString=baha_i_administration_selected_messages_1922_1932_3521e4ac6904cefdca84fce2627329c7-blug.0~baha_i_administration_selected_messages_1922_1932_3521e4ac6904cefdca84fce2627329c7-blug.335))](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-administration_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_793&selectionString=baha_i_administration_selected_messages_1922_1932_3521e4ac6904cefdca84fce2627329c7-blug.335). In [*Unfolding Destiny*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21312) he turned to the Spiritual Assemblies of the West, [on whom Providence had conferred "religious toleration and freedom"](https://oceanlibrary.com/unfolding-destiny_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_486&selectionString=unfolding_destiny_bahai_ocean_en-blhj.0~unfolding_destiny_bahai_ocean_en-blhj.789). He asked them to give the suffering in Persia whatever publicity they could, and described publicity as "our one weapon". He wrote that it would bring lasting solace to the sufferers who continued to uphold their Faith with sublime heroism.

My own reading is that these accounts share a pattern. Persecution is told as a hardship the community meets with steadiness, and in Shoghi Effendi's words it is expected to refine the Cause rather than end it. I can't tell you from these passages how that story continues in recent decades.

If you'd like to pull one thread, read the Síyáh-Chál pages in *The Dawn-Breakers* beside 'Abdu'l-Bahá's 1903 treatise. Together they show how the Faith's earliest and later trials in Iran were understood by those who lived through them.

With warm regards,
Anís

That introduction is commentary. The treatise itself is the primary text, and I didn't find its wording in this search, so I can't quote it here.

**Shoghi Effendi's response.** He wrote "With feelings of burning indignation" about recent events in Persia, and expected that they "cannot but eventually contribute to the strengthening and purification of the Cause" ([link](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-administration_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_793&selectionString=baha_i_administration_selected_messages_1922_1932_3521e4ac6904cefdca84fce2627329c7-blug.0~baha_i_administration_selected_messages_1922_1932_3521e4ac6904cefdca84fce2627329c7-blug.335)) — [*Bahá'í Administration*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20880). In a second letter he thought publicity from the Spiritual Assemblies of the West, "on whom almighty Providence has conferred the inestimable benefits of religious toleration and freedom," would be "most opportune and valuable" ([link](https://oceanlibrary.com/unfolding-destiny_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_486&selectionString=unfolding_destiny_bahai_ocean_en-blhj.0~unfolding_destiny_bahai_ocean_en-blhj.789)) — [*Unfolding Destiny*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21312). The passage breaks off where he names "one weapon," so I won't guess what followed.

**The present.** I didn't find a passage in this search on the situation of the Bahá'ís in Iran today. The House of Justice's messages to them are the place I'd look next, and I can search for them if you'd like.

Of what I found, I'd pull this thread: the Síyáh-Chál accounts in *God Passes By* and *The Dawn-Breakers*, read alongside the treatise on the 1903 events. Reading them together lets you see how the suffering in Iran and the exile that followed became part of the Faith's early story.

The history of the Bahá’í community in Iran is rooted in a profound wave of spiritual emergence followed by generations of enduring persecution.

The origins trace back to May 1844 in Shíráz, when the Báb declared His mission, claiming the authority of the promised Qá'im before eminent Shí'ih ecclesiastics. This declaration initiated the Bábí-Bahá'í movement and set off severe calamities, culminating in the public execution of the Báb at Tabríz on 9 July 1850. As Shoghi Effendi records, the mangled bodies were guarded by four companies of soldiers before being moved, noting that ["On the following morning the Russian Consul in Tabríz visited the spot, and ordered"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_129&selectionString=god_passes_by_ocean_en_6c.0~god_passes_by_ocean_en_6c.1397) [*God Passes By*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21310). Prominent figures like Ṭáhirih were also put to death during these tumultuous early years.

Following the Nayríz and Mázindarán upheavals, Bahá'u'lláh was arrested and taken in chains to the notorious Síyáh-Chál (Black Pit) of Ṭihrán in 1852. Nabil Zarandi records Bahá'u'lláh's own account of being confined there with fellow-prisoners, describing how ["All those who were struck down by the storm that raged during that memorable year in Ṭihrán were Our fellow-prisoners in the Síyáh-C̱hál, where We were confined. We were all huddled together in one cell, our feet in stocks, and around our necks fastened the most galling of chai"](https://oceanlibrary.com/dawn-breakers_nabil/?paraId=para_1875&selectionString=dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_1is.0~dawn-breakers-prod-version_en_1is.1345) [*The Dawn-Breakers*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21308). The Sháh's subsequent edict of expulsion opened a new chapter, beginning Bahá'u'lláh's ministry of nearly forty years in exile, starting in Baghdad.

Throughout the decades, the community expanded—drawing initially on local Muslim populations and later attracting Zoroastrians and Jews—while facing continuous persecution. In the summer of 1903, violent pogroms peaked in cities such as Rasht, Iṣfahán, and Yazd, events which 'Abdu'l-Bahá documented and addressed in a specific treatise detailing the persecutors and the community's suffering.

When later waves of violence struck Persia, Shoghi Effendi wrote with deep emotion, stating, ["With feelings of burning indignation I find myself impelled to acquaint you with various events that have recently transpired in Persia. Though in their immediate effect these happenings may prove gravely disquieting to the followers of the Faith in Persia and elsewhere, yet they cannot but eventually contribute to the strengthening and purification of the Cause we steadfastly love and serve."](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-administration_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_793&selectionString=baha_i_administration_selected_messages_1922_1932_3521e4ac6904cefdca84fce2627329c7-blug.0~baha_i_administration_selected_messages_1922_1932_3521e4ac6904cefdca84fce2627329c7-blug.335) [*Bahá’í Administration*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20880). In the modern era, the Universal House of Justice has frequently addressed the ongoing, systematic persecution of Iranian Bahá'ís by the government, noting their steadfast service and "constructive resilience" in supporting wider society. (These communications from the Universal House of Justice serve as legal and pastoral administration rather than scriptural or doctrinal interpretation).

To explore further, you might look into the accounts of the Síyáh-Chál imprisonment in *The Dawn-Breakers* alongside 'Abdu'l-Bahá's 1903 treatise to see how these trials shaped the identity and endurance of the early community.
