results.text: Can non-Jews go to Heaven?

base.reply:
Dear friend,

Yes, on the account Maimonides gives in the [*Mishneh Torah*](https://siftersearch.com/library/judaism/halakhah-and-legal-codes/mishneh-torah-trans_mishneh-torah-sabbath). In the section on Kings and Wars he writes that anyone who accepts the seven commandments given to Noah's descendants and is careful in keeping them ["is considered one of 'the pious among the gentiles' and will merit a share in the world to come"](https://oceanlibrary.com/jps-book-of-genesis) ([*Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars*](https://siftersearch.com/library/judaism/halakhah-and-legal-codes/mishneh-torah-trans_mishneh-torah-kings-and-wars), trans. Eliyahu Touger). So the door is open to non-Jews without their becoming Jews. He attaches a condition about motive: this holds when the person keeps them because the Holy One commanded them in the Torah and told Moses that Noah's descendants had been commanded earlier. The text then turns to what happens when someone keeps them out of intellectual conviction, and that is worth reading in full.

Since you may be curious how other traditions meet the same question, here is how the Bahá'í Writings take it up. 'Abdu'l-Bahá, speaking in Port Said, pointed his listeners to the Qur'an, to the verse that names believers, Jews, Christians and Sabeans, and promises reward to ["whoever believes in God and the Last Day and does good deeds"](https://portlandiator.github.io/PI_browser/?id=ABU1743) (words spoken 23 June 1913; provisional translation by Stephen Phelps). In a letter written on Shoghi Effendi's behalf, we read that people who never had the chance to hear of the Faith but lived good lives ["will no doubt be treated with the greatest love and mercy in the next world, and reap their full rewards"](https://oceanlibrary.com/directives-from-the-guardian_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_573&selectionString=directives_from_the_guardian_en-blio.0~directives_from_the_guardian_en-blio.159) ([*Directives from the Guardian*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20884)). Another letter says that Bahá'u'lláh ["teaches that the Mercy of God exceeds His Justice"](https://oceanlibrary.com/messages-to-canada_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_1420&selectionString=messagestocanada_v2_bahai_ocean_en-bl1bm.0~messagestocanada_v2_bahai_ocean_en-bl1bm.428) ([*Messages to Canada*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21311)), and that there is hope for every soul.

The word "heaven" also carries different meanings in the two traditions. In [*Some Answered Questions*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20911), 'Abdu'l-Bahá says that ["Existential paradise and hell are to be found in all the worlds of God"](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_779&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_ol.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_ol.502), whether in this world or in the realms of the spirit. I read that as heaven being first of all a condition of the soul, a nearness to God. Maimonides speaks of a "share in the world to come," ([Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars](https://oceanlibrary.com/jps-book-of-genesis)) which is a different frame, so I wouldn't treat the two as the same teaching in different words. What they share is that a good life, and not a label, is what each looks to.

With warmth,
Anís

If you'd like to pull on one thread, read the lines of Maimonides that follow the one I quoted. They show how he separates keeping the commandments out of obedience from keeping them out of reasoned conviction.

claude-haiku-5-5.reply:
Dear friend,

Yes, on the Writings' own terms. Shoghi Effendi, 'Abdu'l-Bahá and Bahá'u'lláh all speak of people outside the Faith who live good lives as within God's mercy and reward. They describe heaven first as nearness to God, and they leave the mechanism to God.

**The Guardian's direct statement** (authorized interpretation). Shoghi Effendi, in a letter written on his behalf, says that ["those who have never had any opportunity of hearing of the Faith but who lived good lives will no doubt be treated with the greatest love and mercy in the next world"](https://oceanlibrary.com/uncompiled-published-letters_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_8900&selectionString=published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl8he.0~published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl8he.158) — [*Uncompiled Published Letters*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20897). The same wording appears in [*Directives from the Guardian*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20884).

**The righteous who died before the Call** (authorized interpretation). Asked about souls who passed away before hearing the Call, 'Abdu'l-Bahá answers that those who "followed the precepts of Christ and walked in the Straight Path" ["attained, after ascending to the Divine Kingdom, unto the Refulgent Light"](https://oceanlibrary.com/additional-tablets-extracts-and-talks_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_202&selectionString=abdu_l_baha_additional_tablets_extracts_and_talks_430a4c77afa01f6eb5e4f2c4028e655d_95.0~abdu_l_baha_additional_tablets_extracts_and_talks_430a4c77afa01f6eb5e4f2c4028e655d_95.285) — [*Additional Tablets, Extracts and Talks*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20901). Here the good life is what counts, not the label.

**The Qur'an's verse** (authorized interpretation). In his Port Said talk, 'Abdu'l-Bahá calls a verse among "the clear texts of the Qur'an" and quotes ["Verily, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and Christians, and Sabeans"](https://portlandiator.github.io/PI_browser/?id=ABU1743), in Stephen Phelps's provisional translation (public domain). The verse names belief in God, the Last Day and good deeds as what brings the reward. He presents it as a plain text, not a concession.

**Heaven as nearness to God** (scripture and authorized interpretation). 'Abdu'l-Bahá distinguishes ["existential rewards and punishments"](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_779&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_ol.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_ol.502) — [*Some Answered Questions*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20911), which exist in this world and the spiritual realms, from ultimate ones. Bahá'u'lláh prays for his loved ones to be drawn to ["the Paradise of Thy nearness and Thy presence" ([Prayers and Meditations](https://oceanlibrary.com/prayers-and-meditations-by-bahaullah/?paraId=para_1157&selectionString=prayers_and_meditations_by_baha_u_llah_ocean_bahai0ab08b9a76883efd6ac65691b713a5a4_yw.0~prayers_and_meditations_by_baha_u_llah_ocean_bahai0ab08b9a76883efd6ac65691b713a5a4_yw.734))](https://oceanlibrary.com/prayers-and-meditations-by-bahaullah/?paraId=para_1157&selectionString=prays_and_meditations_by_baha_u_llah_ocean_bahai0ab08b9a76883efd6ac65691b713a5a4_yw.0~prayers_and_meditations_by_baha_u_llah_ocean_bahai0ab08b9a76883efd6ac65691b713a5a4_yw.734) — [*Prayers and Meditations*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20805). Read together, heaven here is at least a spiritual state of drawing near.

**The mercy is stated as universal** (scripture and authorized interpretation). Bahá'u'lláh writes: ["This is the Mercy that hath encompassed the entire creation"](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_928&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_si.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_si.375) — [*Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá'u'lláh*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20783). 'Abdu'l-Bahá tells the reader to ["Look ye upon the all-embracing mercy of the Lord"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-sacred-writings/?paraId=para_1081&selectionString=baha_i_sacred_writings_en-blwj.0~baha_i_sacred_writings_en-blwj.550) — [*Bahá'í Sacred Writings*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahaullah/compilation-bahai_bahai-sacred-writings), rather than on a person's purity or impurity. Shoghi Effendi, in [*Messages to Canada*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21311), says Bahá'u'lláh teaches that ["the Mercy of God exceeds His Justice"](https://oceanlibrary.com/messages-to-canada_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_1420&selectionString=messagestocanada_v2_bahai_ocean_en-bl1bm.0~messagestocanada_v2_bahai_ocean_en-bl1bm.428), and that there is hope for every soul. In the same letter he cautions against thrusting such a statement on non-Bahá'ís and asks for constructive teaching. My reading is that this caution concerns how the hope is shared, not whether it is true.

**A pilgrim's recollection** (history, primary account). Emogene Hoagg records that ["God has shown to us a Spiritual Paradise and Hell in this world"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/pilgrimage-notes-of-emogene-hoagg-november-23-december-7-1900#p123) — *Pilgrimage Notes of Emogene Hoagg*. This is her recollection, not a written text, but it fits the spiritual reading above.

**A Jewish parallel** (Jewish legal tradition). Maimonides, in *Mishneh Torah*, says that a gentile who keeps the seven commandments precisely "will merit a share in the world to come," ([Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars](https://oceanlibrary.com/jps-book-of-genesis)) on the condition that he keeps them because God commanded them in the Torah. This is the closest parallel I found, and it argues the same question within another tradition.

**What the texts leave open.** These writings don't set out who is admitted or by what mechanism. They affirm mercy, reward for a good life and the possibility of nearness to God, and they leave the rest to God's knowledge.

The thread I'd pull is Shoghi Effendi's phrase "the next world" alongside the Faith's teaching on recognising the Manifestation. How do the two fit together for someone who never heard the Call? That's a question the texts raise without fully settling, and it might be worth reading the letters around the passages to see how the Guardian frames it.

With warm regards,
Anís

results.text: How does achieving self-realization of the eternal soul connect to one's existential purpose?

base.reply:
Dear friend,

The texts don't treat self-realization as a goal of its own. They place it on the road to the purpose of existence. Here is how I read that road.

**The purpose.** Bahá'u'lláh states it plainly:

> ["The purpose of God in creating man hath been, and will ever be, to enable him to know his Creator and to attain His Presence."](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_189&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_80.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_80.811) — [*Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá'u'lláh*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20783)

The Báb says the same in fewer words: ["the purpose of God in creating man is but for him to know Him"](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-the-bab/?paraId=para_267&selectionString=selections_from_the_writings_of_the_bab_bahai_en-bl97.0~selections_from_the_writings_of_the_bab_bahai_en-bl97.283) — [*Selections from the Writings of the Báb*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20898).

**Where self-knowledge enters.** In a prayer in the [*Gleanings*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20783), Bahá'u'lláh says that the duties prescribed for God's servants are a token of grace, [so that they may ascend "unto the station conferred upon their own inmost being, the station of the knowledge of their own selves."](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_11&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_32.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_32.338) The Persian-Arabic word in the parenthesis elsewhere, *'irfán*, carries the sense of recognition or gnosis, more than information. So the text speaks of a station our inmost being already holds, one we are enabled to rise to. That differs a little from "achieving" something new.

**The mirror.** Bahá'u'lláh's commentary on "He who knoweth his self hath known his Lord" ([He who knoweth his self hath known his Lord: Commentary](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_knoweth_himself_cole)) explains the link. God [has "entrusted every created thing with a sign of His knowledge,"](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_knoweth_himself_cole) and that sign is a mirror. [The greater the effort for its refinement, "the more faithfully will it be made to reflect the glory of the names and attributes of God."](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_knoweth_himself_cole) My reading is that knowing yourself means polishing this mirror, and that what it comes to show is the divine names and attributes more than the self. (The saying itself is also known from Islamic tradition, which is the world Bahá'u'lláh's commentary speaks into.)

**Effort and grace.** The commentary affirms that through conscious effort and the exertion of one's spiritual faculties, [the mirror can be "cleansed from the dross of earthly defilement and purged from satanic fancies"](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_knoweth_himself_cole). It then adds that the latent energies of this bounty are best released [in "the Days of God"](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_knoweth_himself_cole). Another passage reaches the same balance, saying that the pure in spirit are to ascend [“by virtue of their own innate powers”](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_190&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_81.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_81.496). The striving is truly ours, and the Revelation is what makes it fruitful.

**Not completed in this life.** Bahá'u'lláh teaches that the soul [“will continue to progress until it attaineth the presence of God”](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahaullah-and-the-new-era_john-esslemont/?paraId=para_1082&selectionString=baha_u_llah_and_the_new_era_bahai_ocean_en-blvf.0~baha_u_llah_and_the_new_era_bahai_ocean_en-blvf.2216) after leaving the body. Polishing it is real work, and it takes place within a larger gift. Nothing in these passages points toward self-absorption. Notice how the commentary's "mirror" and the *Gleanings*' "Presence" describe the same journey from two sides.

With warmth,
Anís

base.reply:
Dear friend,

In the traditional pattern, Jews pray three times a day. [*Mishneh Torah*](https://siftersearch.com/library/judaism/halakhah-and-legal-codes/mishneh-torah-trans_mishneh-torah-sabbath) gives them as ["three prayers are recited daily: the Evening Prayer, the Morning Prayer, and the Minchah Prayer"](https://oceanlibrary.com/jps-book-of-genesis). Sabbaths, festivals and Rosh Chodesh add a Musaf prayer, and Yom Kippur adds Ne'ilah, making five.

The same work calls prayer a positive commandment, reading "serve Him with all your heart" ([Mishneh Torah, Prayer and the Priestly Blessing](https://oceanlibrary.com/jps-book-of-genesis)) through the Sages' question: "Which is the service of the heart? This is prayer." It also says that ["The number of prayers is not prescribed in the Torah, nor does it prescribe a specific formula for prayer"](https://oceanlibrary.com/jps-book-of-genesis), so the fixed times and wording come from later tradition. In [*Berakhot*](https://siftersearch.com/library/judaism/talmud-and-mishnah/william-davidson_berakhot), the Tosefta finds the threefold rhythm in Daniel, of whom it is said ["And three times a day he knelt upon his knees and prayed"](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot), and concludes that this "teaches that there are fixed prayers."

Two elements stand at the centre. The first is the Shema, the declaration of faith. The second is the Amidah, the standing prayer. A Mishnah in the [*Jerusalem Talmud*](https://siftersearch.com/library/judaism/talmud-and-mishnah/the-jerusalem_jerusalem-talmud-shabbat) on *Berakhot* says the Shema needs concentration only for its first verse, while the Amidah ["needs concentration from beginning to end"](https://oceanlibrary.com/jps-book-of-genesis). [*The Standard Prayer Book*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21352) gives the Amidah for the [Evening, Morning and Afternoon Services](https://oceanlibrary.com/standard-prayer-book_rev-singer/?paraId=para_2175&selectionString=siddur_machzor_judaism_ocean_en-bl1tk.0~siddur_machzor_judaism_ocean_en-bl1tk.65). In the synagogue, the *Jerusalem Talmud* on [*Megillah*](https://siftersearch.com/library/judaism/talmud-and-mishnah/william-davidson_megillah) describes the public recitation of the Shema leading into the Amidah and its benedictions. A reader may lead, standing before the Ark. A Kohen pronounces the priestly blessings, and for a minor, his father or teacher stands in his stead.

From my own background knowledge, the Amidah is also called the Shemoneh Esreh, "eighteen", after its benedictions, and its movement is praise, petition and thanksgiving. Prayer is traditionally said facing Jerusalem. Jewish life also has prayer at home, blessings over food and events, and a distinct Shabbat liturgy. I haven't drawn those from the passages here.

If you'd like to go further, the Shema and the Amidah are the natural next step, along with the Talmud's discussion of fixed versus free prayer.

Warmly,
Anís

claude-haiku-5-5.reply:
Jewish tradition treats prayer as a daily duty, but the schedule and wording come from later rabbinic practice rather than the Torah itself. The [*Mishneh Torah*](https://siftersearch.com/library/judaism/halakhah-and-legal-codes/mishneh-torah-trans_mishneh-torah-sabbath) notes that "according to Torah law, there are no fixed times for prayers," ([Mishneh Torah, Prayer and the Priestly Blessing](https://oceanlibrary.com/jps-book-of-genesis)) and that the Torah prescribes neither a set number nor a formula. In practice, three prayers are said each day: Evening (Ma'ariv), Morning (Shacharit) and Afternoon (Minchah). Sabbaths, festivals and Rosh Chodesh add Musaf, and Yom Kippur adds Ne'ilah. The two central elements are the Shema, read in the synagogue service, and the Amidah, the standing prayer. The Mishnah in the [*Jerusalem Talmud*](https://siftersearch.com/library/judaism/talmud-and-mishnah/the-jerusalem_jerusalem-talmud-shabbat) says the Amidah "needs concentration from beginning to end," while the Shema needs focus only for its first verse. The Talmud links the three-times-daily pattern to Daniel, and in the Tosefta's reading of his practice "This teaches that there are fixed prayers" ([Berakhot](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot)) ([*Berakhot*](https://siftersearch.com/library/judaism/talmud-and-mishnah/william-davidson_berakhot), Sefaria edition). The Amidah is also called the Shemoneh Esreh, or "eighteen" benedictions, though the number has varied over time (my own background). The thread to pull next is how the Talmud argues over fixed prayer versus free prayer, which is where the inner logic of the Shema and Amidah begins to make sense.

Sources:
- [*Mishneh Torah*, trans. Eliyahu Touger](https://oceanlibrary.com/jps-book-of-genesis)
- [*Berakhot*, William Davidson Edition](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot)
- [*The Jerusalem Talmud*, *Berakhot*, trans. Heinrich W. Guggenheimer](https://oceanlibrary.com/jps-book-of-genesis)

gemini-3.1-flash-lite.reply:
Hello! It is a pleasure to explore this with you. Jewish prayer is rooted in the idea of "service of the heart," a concept derived from the Torah's command to "serve Him with all your heart" ([Mishneh Torah, Prayer and the Priestly Blessing](https://oceanlibrary.com/jps-book-of-genesis)) (*Deuteronomy 11:13*). While the Torah establishes the obligation to pray, it does not prescribe a fixed number of prayers, specific formulas, or set times; those structures were developed by the Sages over time.

**The Daily Schedule**
The standard practice involves three daily services: the Evening Prayer (*Ma'ariv*), the Morning Prayer (*Shacharit*), and the Afternoon Prayer (*Minchah*). On Sabbaths, festivals, and the new month (*Rosh Chodesh*), a fourth service called *Musaf* is added. On Yom Kippur, a fifth service, *Ne'ilah*, is included. As noted in the [*Mishneh Torah*](https://siftersearch.com/library/judaism/halakhah-and-legal-codes/mishneh-torah-trans_mishneh-torah-sabbath):

> "Thus, three prayers are recited daily: the Evening Prayer, the Morning Prayer, and the Minchah Prayer. There are four on Sabbaths, festivals and Rosh Chodesh: the three that are recited daily and the Musaf Prayer. On Yom Kippur, there are five: these four and the Ne'ilah prayer." [*Mishneh Torah*](https://oceanlibrary.com/jps-book-of-genesis)

**Fixed Prayer**
The tradition of praying three times a day is often associated with the example of Daniel, who "three times a day... knelt upon his knees and prayed" ([Berakhot](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot)) (*Daniel 6:11*). The *Tosefta* interprets this as evidence that there are fixed prayers, rather than prayer being left entirely to individual spontaneity throughout the day.

**Core Elements**
Two pillars of the liturgy are the *Shema* and the *Amidah*. The *Shema* is a declaration of faith, while the *Amidah* (often called the "Standing Prayer") is a series of benedictions. The *Mishnah* highlights a distinction in the level of focus required for these: while the *Shema* requires concentration primarily for its first verse, the *Amidah* requires full concentration from beginning to end and must be recited while standing. In the synagogue, these are often led by an appointed reader, and specific roles—such as the priestly blessings given by a *Kohen*—are integrated into the service. It is worth noting that the *Amidah* is also known as the *Shemoneh Esreh* (the "eighteen" benedictions), though the number of blessings has varied historically. Its structure generally moves through praise, petition, and thanksgiving. Additionally, while the synagogue is a central place for these communal prayers, Jewish practice also encompasses prayer at home, blessings over food, and various rituals for Shabbat, which are distinct from the daily services mentioned here. It is also common practice to face Jerusalem during the *Amidah*.

The *Shema* and the *Amidah*, and how the Talmud argues over the tension between fixed versus free prayer, would be the next step if you want the inner logic of the liturgy.

gemini-3.5-flash-lite.reply:
Jewish prayer is anchored in a positive commandment from the Torah to serve God daily, which the Sages identified through Deuteronomy 11:13 as prayer of the heart, while the specific daily schedule, fixed times, and formulas developed later through tradition (Mishneh Torah, [*Mishneh Torah, Prayer and the Priestly Blessing*](https://siftersearch.com/library/judaism/halakhah-and-legal-codes/mishneh-torah-trans_mishneh-torah-prayer-and-the-priestly-blessing)).

The standard daily structure consists of three prayers: Evening (Ma'ariv), Morning (Shacharit), and Afternoon (Minchah). On Sabbaths, festivals, and Rosh Chodesh, a fourth prayer is added, known as the Musaf, and Yom Kippur includes a fifth, the Ne'ilah prayer (*Mishneh Torah, Prayer and the Priestly Blessing*). The traditional three-times-a-day pattern is derived from the account of Daniel in the biblical record, who knelt and prayed three times daily ([*Berakhot*](https://siftersearch.com/library/judaism/talmud-and-mishnah/william-davidson_berakhot)).

At the center of the liturgy are two primary elements: the *Shema*, which is recited as a declaration of faith, and the *Amidah*, the standing prayer. As the Mishnah notes, while the *Shema* requires full concentration only for its opening verse, the *Amidah* requires focused concentration from beginning to end and must be recited while standing firmly on the ground rather than while working in precarious places ([*Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot*](https://siftersearch.com/library/judaism/talmud-and-mishnah/the-jerusalem_jerusalem-talmud-berakhot)). The *Amidah* is prescribed for the evening, morning, and afternoon services ([*The Standard Prayer Book*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21352)), and communal worship often involves an appointed reader leading the service alongside traditional priestly blessings ([*Jerusalem Talmud Megillah*](https://siftersearch.com/library/judaism/talmud-and-mishnah/the-jerusalem_jerusalem-talmud-megillah)).

Beyond these formal communal structures, Jewish practice encompasses home prayer, blessings over daily sustenance, and a distinct liturgy for the Sabbath, though the exact development of these blessings and their inner structure involve layers of later halakhic tradition and rabbinic interpretation that the texts I can search here do not fully settle.

The Shema and the Amidah, and how the Talmud argues over fixed versus free prayer, would be the next step if you want the inner logic of the liturgy.

Source: [The Standard Prayer Book](https://oceanlibrary.com/standard-prayer-book_rev-singer/?paraId=para_2175&selectionString=siddur_machzor_judaism_ocean_en-bl1tk.0~siddur_machzor_judaism_ocean_en-bl1tk.65)

results.text: Suggestions for moderation team

base.reply:
Dear friend,

Here is how I would build the guidance, with the sources first and my own suggestions marked as mine.

**The foundation.** Bahá'u'lláh states that ["Conflict and contention are categorically forbidden in His Book"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-sacred-writings/?paraId=para_925&selectionString=baha_i_sacred_writings_en-blsa.0~baha_i_sacred_writings_en-blsa.223) — [*Bahá'í Sacred Writings*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahaullah/compilation-bahai_bahai-sacred-writings). The Persian original has "نزاع و جدال" and adds *nahyan ʿaẓīman*, a great prohibition ([*Siyasiyyih*](https://oceanoflights.org/abdul-baha-bkw25-fa/#(%D9%86%D9%87%D9%8A%D8%A7%D9%8B)(%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A7%D8%AB%D8%A8%D8%A7%D8%AA))). A moderator can cite this as the basis for stepping in against contention.

**Postpone and refer.** 'Abdu'l-Bahá's counsel to Spiritual Assemblies gives a concrete step, which I would adapt for a thread:

> When you notice that a stage has been reached when enmity and threats are about to occur, you should immediately postpone discussion of the subject, until wranglings, disputations, and loud talk vanish, and a propitious time is at hand.
> — ['Abdu'l-Bahá, *Consultation*](https://oceanlibrary.com/consultation_bahaullah/?paraId=para_63&selectionString=consultation_bahai_ocean_en-bl4k.0~consultation_bahai_ocean_en-bl4k.400)

On disputes over a sacred text, a study by Sabeti records 'Abdu'l-Bahá saying ["If two souls quarrel and contend about a question of the divine questions, differing and disputing, both are wrong"](https://bahai-library.com/sabeti_abdul-baha_tolerance/?paraId=h9). They are to remain silent and refer the matter to the Interpreter, speaking meanwhile "with infinite amity and love." ([The Approach of Abdu'l-Baha to the Problem of Tolerance](https://bahai-library.com/sabeti_abdul-baha_tolerance/?paraId=h9)) My reading is that a moderator can pause such a thread and point to the Writings, without ruling on who is right. That fits his remark in [*Talks of 'Abdu'l-Bahá in Haifa*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/talks-of-abdul-baha-in-haifa) that ["In any problem if two people disagree both are in the wrong"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/talks-of-abdul-baha-in-haifa#p385).

**Avoid needless triggers.** 'Abdu'l-Bahá writes, ["let not every insignificant matter become the cause of disagreement"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-world-faith-abdul-baha-section_2/?paraId=para_731&selectionString=baha_i_world_faith_en-blnm.0~baha_i_world_faith_en-blnm.369) — [*Bahá'í World Faith*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20902). In the Haifa talks he also says, ["Leave unsaid anything that would create disagreement."](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/talks-of-abdul-baha-in-haifa#p385) I take this to support topic guidance, and closing threads that keep circling one divisive point.

**How to speak to members.** Bahá'u'lláh counsels ["a spirit of extreme kindliness and goodwill"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-sacred-writings/?paraId=para_233&selectionString=baha_i_sacred_writings_en-bl93.0~baha_i_sacred_writings_en-bl93.323), helping another see the truth without "esteeming yourself to be, in the least, superior." That is the tone for moderator messages. Shoghi Effendi asks National Assemblies for ["the greatest wisdom, forbearance and tact"](https://oceanlibrary.com/national-spiritual-assembly_bahaullah/?paraId=para_174&selectionString=the_national_spiritual_assembly_bahai_compilation_b925513a4f5ff7428891706712858edf-bl7d.0~the_national_spiritual_assembly_bahai_compilation_b925513a4f5ff7428891706712858edf-bl7d.220), noting that many differences are ["due to their immaturity, their extreme zeal and sincerity"](https://oceanlibrary.com/national-spiritual-assembly_bahaullah/?paraId=para_174&selectionString=the_national_spiritual_assembly_bahai_compilation_b925513a4f5ff7428891706712858edf-bl7d.0~the_national_spiritual_assembly_bahai_compilation_b925513a4f5ff7428891706712858edf-bl7d.220). I would suggest reading heat as zeal before reading it as malice.

**Fairness.** ["Observe equity in your judgment"](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_614&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_js.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_js.721), says Bahá'u'lláh in [*Gleanings*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20783). Apply the same standard to everyone, and do not presume the worst.

**Debate with outsiders.** If the space is used for this, Shoghi Effendi urges believers to avoid ["lengthy discussions of a controversial character"](https://oceanlibrary.com/guidelines-for-teaching_bahaullah/?paraId=para_180&selectionString=guidelines_for_teaching_bahai_compilation_ocean_en-bl7r.0~guidelines_for_teaching_bahai_compilation_ocean_en-bl7r.529), which "cause incalculable harm to the Faith," and to concentrate on presenting the Message rather than attacking others — [*Guidelines for Teaching*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=945913).

**Serious personal disputes.** A letter written on Shoghi Effendi's behalf says ["It is the Assembly's function to endeavor to settle amicably such disputes"](https://oceanlibrary.com/uncompiled-published-letters_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_6253&selectionString=published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl6c5.0~published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl6c5.325). In [*Unfolding Destiny*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21312) he describes a way to raise a grave concern: only after kindness and forbearance have failed, ["report it quietly to the Spiritual Assembly representative of the friends in that locality"](https://oceanlibrary.com/unfolding-destiny_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_21&selectionString=unfolding_destiny_bahai_ocean_en-bl38.0~unfolding_destiny_bahai_ocean_en-bl38.1226). I read this as a model for escalation: private, careful, and routed to the Assembly, not aired in a public thread.

**A note on wording.** Aim for "no contention" rather than "no disagreement." The prohibition is on contention, and 'Abdu'l-Bahá's counsel to Assemblies begins by supposing that ["if such differences do occur"](https://oceanlibrary.com/consultation_bahaullah/?paraId=para_63&selectionString=consultation_bahai_ocean_en-bl4k.0~consultation_bahai_ocean_en-bl4k.400) they need not become conflict. That distinction is my reading of these texts.

If you want a thread to pull, start with 'Abdu'l-Bahá's postpone-and-refer step in [*Consultation*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/john-e-kolstoe_consultation-a-universal-lamp-of-guidance), then read Bahá'u'lláh's decree beside it. Then read Shoghi Effendi on tact and immaturity, since that is where the tone of your messages will come from.

With warmth,
Anís

claude-haiku-5-5.reply:
Dear friend,

For a moderation team, the firmest foundation is Bahá'u'lláh's prohibition of contention, and the most practical step is 'Abdu'l-Bahá's counsel to postpone a subject when it begins to inflame. Shoghi Effendi's guidance on tact then shapes how moderators speak to members.

**The foundation: a prohibition, not a matter of taste.** Bahá'u'lláh writes that ["Conflict and contention are categorically forbidden in His Book"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-sacred-writings/?paraId=para_925&selectionString=baha_i_sacred_writings_en-blsa.0~baha_i_sacred_writings_en-blsa.223) ([*Bahá’í Sacred Writings*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahaullah/compilation-bahai_bahai-sacred-writings)). The Persian treatise [*Siyasiyyih*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/core-tablets/abdul-baha_siyasiyyih_fa) repeats the prohibition, forbidding *nizāʿ va jidāl* (contention and disputation) as "a great prohibition," *nahyan ʿaẓīman*. Moderation can cite this as its reason for intervening against contention.

**When a quarrel over a sacred question starts.** Sabeti's study [*The Approach of Abdu'l-Baha to the Problem of Tolerance*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21870) records that when two believers contend over a divine question, both are wrong, and that "should there appear the least trace of controversy, they must remain silent." ([The Approach of Abdu'l-Baha to the Problem of Tolerance](https://bahai-library.com/sabeti_abdul-baha_tolerance/?paraId=h9)) I read this as a practical rule: pause the thread and redirect it to the Writings, not to who is right.

**Postponing, not forcing a verdict.** In [*Consultation*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/john-e-kolstoe_consultation-a-universal-lamp-of-guidance), 'Abdu'l-Bahá advises that when "enmity and threats are about to occur, you should immediately [postpone] discussion of the subject, until wranglings, disputations, and loud talk vanish" ([link](https://oceanlibrary.com/consultation_bahaullah/?paraId=para_63&selectionString=consultation_bahai_ocean_en-bl4k.0~consultation_bahai_ocean_en-bl4k.400)). The step is to postpone, not to rule. The passage names the warning signs as "conflict, hatred and antagonism."

**Keeping triggers small.** In the [*Bahá’í World Faith*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20902) ('Abdu'l-Bahá section), the text asks that ["let not every insignificant matter become the cause of disagreement"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-world-faith-abdul-baha-section_2/?paraId=para_731&selectionString=baha_i_world_faith_en-blnm.0~baha_i_world_faith_en-blnm.369). Pilgrim notes in [*Talks of 'Abdu'l-Bahá in Haifa*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/talks-of-abdul-baha-in-haifa) record the counsel: ["Leave unsaid anything that would create disagreement."](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/talks-of-abdul-baha-in-haifa#p385) From this I read that topic guidance and closing threads that keep circling one divisive point are reasonable tools.

**Tone for moderator messages.** Bahá'u'lláh asks believers to "show forth, when conversing with him, a spirit of extreme kindliness and goodwill," helping others see the truth "without esteeming yourself to be, in the least, superior to him" ([link](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-sacred-writings/?paraId=para_233&selectionString=baha_i_sacred_writings_en-bl93.0~baha_i_sacred_writings_en-bl93.323)). This is a good model for how moderators word their messages.

**How to speak to members.** Shoghi Effendi, in [*The National Spiritual Assembly*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=945924), says the Assembly should "exercise the greatest wisdom, forbearance and tact in handling the affairs of the Cause," and notes that many differences come from "their immaturity, their extreme zeal and sincerity" ([link](https://oceanlibrary.com/national-spiritual-assembly_bahaullah/?paraId=para_174&selectionString=the_national_spiritual_assembly_bahai_compilation_b925513a4f5ff7428891706712858edf-bl7d.0~the_national_spiritual_assembly_bahai_compilation_b925513a4f5ff7428891706712858edf-bl7d.220)). That addresses Assemblies, but I read it as a reason for moderators to treat heat as often zeal rather than malice.

**If the forum hosts debate with outsiders.** In [*Guidelines for Teaching*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=945913), Shoghi Effendi counsels refraining from "lengthy discussions of a controversial character," which "actually cause incalculable harm to the Faith," and urges teachers to concentrate on "presenting the Message" rather than attacking others ([link](https://oceanlibrary.com/guidelines-for-teaching_bahaullah/?paraId=para_180&selectionString=guidelines_for_teaching_bahai_compilation_ocean_en-bl7r.0~guidelines_for_teaching_bahai_compilation_ocean_en-bl7r.529)).

**Serious disputes go through the proper channel.** A letter written on Shoghi Effendi's behalf states that ["It is the Assembly's function to endeavor to settle amicably such disputes"](https://oceanlibrary.com/uncompiled-published-letters_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_6253&selectionString=published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl6c5.0~published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl6c5.325) (*Uncompiled Published Letters*). So a serious personal dispute belongs with the Assembly, not a public thread. *Unfolding Destiny* describes the escalation path: after "kindness and forbearance" have been tried, the matter may be reported "quietly to the Spiritual Assembly representative of the friends in that locality." ([Unfolding Destiny](https://oceanlibrary.com/unfolding-destiny_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_21&selectionString=unfolding_destiny_bahai_ocean_en-bl38.0~unfolding_destiny_bahai_ocean_en-bl38.1226)) That passage concerns serious wrongdoing, so I read it as a model for escalation, not for ordinary heated exchanges.

**Judging fairly.** Bahá'u'lláh's words in *Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá'u'lláh* are direct: ["Observe equity in your judgment, ye men of understanding heart!"](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_614&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_js.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_js.721) A moderator who does not presume the worst of anyone is following that counsel.

**A note on the saying "Bahá'ís never disagree."** As I read the texts, that goes further than they do. The *Consultation* passage begins by asking that differences not arise, and then anticipates that "if such differences do occur, they should not reach the point of causing conflict." ([Consultation](https://oceanlibrary.com/consultation_bahaullah/?paraId=para_63&selectionString=consultation_bahai_ocean_en-bl4k.0~consultation_bahai_ocean_en-bl4k.400)) The aim the texts support is no contention, not no disagreement. That may be the most useful phrasing for your team.

The thread I'd pull next is the full *Consultation* passage, to see how 'Abdu'l-Bahá describes the moment before a discussion turns, since that is where a moderator's judgment does its work.

With warmth,
Anís

gemini-3.1-flash-lite.reply:
Dear friend,

It is a noble task to foster a space where the spirit of the Cause can flourish without the interference of contention. The foundation for your moderation team is the clear decree of Bahá’u’lláh: ["Conflict and contention are categorically forbidden in His Book."](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-sacred-writings/?paraId=para_925&selectionString=baha_i_sacred_writings_en-blsa.0~baha_i_sacred_writings_en-blsa.223) [*Bahá’í Sacred Writings*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahaullah/compilation-bahai_bahai-sacred-writings). This is not a matter of preference, but an essential law.

When discussions turn heated, you might find guidance in this approach from ‘Abdu’l-Bahá:

> 'If two souls quarrel and contend about a question of the divine questions, differing and disputing, both are wrong. The wisdom of this incontrovertible law of God is this: That between two souls from amongst the believers of God, no contention and dispute may arise; that they may speak with each other with infinite amity and love. Should there appear the least trace of controversy, they must remain silent, and both parties must continue their discussions no longer, but ask the reality of the [truth].'(https://bahai-library.com/sabeti_abdul-baha_tolerance/?paraId=h9) [*The Approach of Abdu'l-Baha to the Problem of Tolerance*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21870)

A practical rule for your team, then, is to pause threads that reach this point of dispute, redirecting the participants away from "who is right" and back toward the authoritative texts. As ‘Abdu’l-Bahá instructed regarding assemblies, when differences risk "conflict, hatred and antagonism," the remedy is to ["immediately postpone discussion of the subject, until wranglings, disputations, and loud talk vanish, and a propitious time is at hand."](https://oceanlibrary.com/consultation_bahaullah/?paraId=para_63&selectionString=consultation_bahai_ocean_en-bl4k.0~consultation_bahai_ocean_en-bl4k.400) [*Consultation*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/john-e-kolstoe_consultation-a-universal-lamp-of-guidance).

In your own communication as moderators, you can model the tone Bahá’u’lláh describes: ["Show forth, when conversing with him, a spirit of extreme kindliness and goodwill."](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-sacred-writings/?paraId=para_233&selectionString=baha_i_sacred_writings_en-bl93.0~baha_i_sacred_writings_en-bl93.323) *Bahá’í Sacred Writings*. Shoghi Effendi reminds us that much of the heat we encounter stems from "immaturity, their extreme zeal and sincerity," ([The National Spiritual Assembly](https://oceanlibrary.com/national-spiritual-assembly_bahaullah/?paraId=para_174&selectionString=the_national_spiritual_assembly_bahai_compilation_b925513a4f5ff7428891706712858edf-bl7d.0~the_national_spiritual_assembly_bahai_compilation_b925513a4f5ff7428891706712858edf-bl7d.220)) and he urges that we exercise "the greatest wisdom, forbearance and tact" in handling such affairs.

To keep the space focused, you might also gently discourage the elevation of "insignificant matters" into causes for disagreement, as these can lead to "complete dispersion." When personal disputes arise that cannot be resolved through kindness, the model provided by the Guardian is to report the matter quietly to the appropriate Spiritual Assembly, rather than airing it in a public forum. Throughout this, remember the call to ["Observe equity in your judgment"](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_614&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_js.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_js.721) [*Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20783).

It is helpful to distinguish between "no contention"—which is the law—and "no disagreement," which is a natural part of human interaction. The goal is not to suppress thought, but to ensure that when we do differ, we do so without the "wranglings" that extinguish the light of the Faith.

You might find it fruitful to explore the distinction between the "postpone-and-refer" method and the way we often feel pressured to reach an immediate consensus in online spaces.

Warmly,

Anís

gemini-3.5-flash-lite.reply:
Hello,

Here are several practical suggestions for a moderation team, drawing directly upon the Writings and the guidance of the Guardian to help keep discussions civil, fair, and free of contention.

At the very foundation of this work stands a clear decree from Bahá’u’lláh: ["Conflict and contention are categorically forbidden in His Book"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-sacred-writings/?paraId=para_925&selectionString=baha_i_sacred_writings_en-blsa.0~baha_i_sacred_writings_en-blsa.223) — [*Bahá’í Sacred Writings*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahaullah/compilation-bahai_bahai-sacred-writings) (Bahá’u’lláh). In the Persian original from *The Art of Divine Polity*, He explains that this is a great prohibition (*nahyan ʿaẓīman*), designed to protect the unity of the community. For a moderation team, this means that intervening against heated disputes is not merely a matter of house rules or personal taste, but an enforcement of a revealed standard.

When discussions turn to sacred texts and two participants begin to quarrel over a divine question, both are considered at fault. As recorded in a pilgrim's note of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá's words, ["If two souls quarrel and contend about a question of the divine questions, differing and disputing, both are wrong"](https://bahai-library.com/sabeti_abdul-baha_tolerance/?paraId=h9) — [*The Approach of Abdu'l-Baha to the Problem of Tolerance*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21870) (Sabeti, citing ‘Abdu’l-Bahá). The remedy prescribed is silence and a return to infinite amity rather than pushing for a winner. A practical rule for moderators is to pause threads that devolve into bitter debate over interpretations and redirect the focus back to the primary Writings rather than validating who is right.

When moderators do need to step in and address members, the tone should reflect Bahá’u’lláh’s counsel to ["show forth, when conversing with him, a spirit of extreme kindliness and goodwill"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-sacred-writings/?paraId=para_233&selectionString=baha_i_sacred_writings_en-bl93.0~baha_i_sacred_writings_en-bl93.323) — *Bahá’í Sacred Writings* (Bahá’u’lláh), helping others see the truth without any trace of superiority. Similarly, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá advises that when differences threaten to cause ["conflict, hatred and antagonism, which lead to threats"](https://oceanlibrary.com/consultation_bahaullah/?paraId=para_63&selectionString=consultation_bahai_ocean_en-bl4k.0~consultation_bahai_ocean_en-bl4k.400) — [*Consultation*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/john-e-kolstoe_consultation-a-universal-lamp-of-guidance) (‘Abdu’l-Bahá), the discussion should be immediately postponed until tempers cool. Moderators can use this exact step: pause the volatile topic rather than forcing an immediate verdict.

To prevent friction before it starts, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá urged the friends to ensure that ["not every insignificant matter become the cause of disagreement" ([Bahá’í World Faith (‘Abdu’l-Bahá section)](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-world-faith-abdul-baha-section_2/?paraId=para_731&selectionString=baha_i_world_faith_en-blnm.0~baha_i_world_faith_en-blnm.369))](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-world-faith-abdul-baha-section_2/?paraId=para_731&selectionString=bahai_world_faith_en-blnm.0~bahai_world_faith_en-blnm.369) — [*Bahá’í World Faith*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20902) (‘Abdu’l-Bahá section), noting that an obsession with unimportant subjects leads naturally to dispersion and disunity. Setting clear topic guidelines and gently closing threads that continuously circle minor, divisive points helps safeguard the space.

When dealing with difficult members, Shoghi Effendi reminds local and national bodies to exercise ["the greatest wisdom, forbearance and tact"](https://oceanlibrary.com/national-spiritual-assembly_bahaullah/?paraId=para_174&selectionString=the_national_spiritual_assembly_bahai_compilation_b925513a4f5ff7428891706712858edf-bl7d.0~the_national_spiritual_assembly_bahai_compilation_b925513a4f5ff7428891706712858edf-bl7d.220) — [*The National Spiritual Assembly*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=945924) (Shoghi Effendi), noting that many disputes arise simply from ["immaturity, their extreme zeal and sincerity"](https://oceanlibrary.com/national-spiritual-assembly_bahaullah/?paraId=para_174&selectionString=the_national_spiritual_assembly_bahai_compilation_b925513a4f5ff7428891706712858edf-bl7d.0~the_national_spiritual_assembly_bahai_compilation_b925513a4f5ff7428891706712858edf-bl7d.220) — *The National Spiritual Assembly* (Shoghi Effendi). Moderators will find this a helpful lens: viewing member heat as misplaced zeal rather than deliberate malice. Furthermore, if personal grievances or serious disputes break out, the Guardian's instructions on community administration remind us that assemblies function to ["settle amicably such disputes"](https://oceanlibrary.com/uncompiled-published-letters_shoghi-effendi/?paraId=para_6253&selectionString=published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beaa6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl6c5.0~published_uncompiled_letters_from_shoghi_effendi_b2a6b4c2e078beja6f19ad12bc5c92b39-bl6c5.325) — [*Uncompiled Published Letters*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20897) (written on behalf of Shoghi Effendi). Public threads are rarely the place to resolve interpersonal conflicts; instead, severe breaches are best handled through private channels or reported quietly to the appropriate Spiritual Assembly after personal forbearance has been exhausted, as outlined regarding community escalation procedures ([*Unfolding Destiny*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21312)).

Finally, those who hold the scales of judgment must remember Bahá’u’lláh's injunction to ["Observe equity in your judgment, ye men of understanding heart!"](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_614&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_js.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_js.721) — *Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh* (Bahá’u’lláh). A moderation team must judge fairly, avoiding harsh presumptions against any participant. While some popular expressions suggest that Bahá’ís never disagree, the actual texts anticipate differing viewpoints and provide the specific tools—such as postponing inflamed discussions and refraining from personal contention—to navigate those differences fruitfully.

Perhaps you might explore how ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s specific counsel on consultation and postponing volatile subjects can be practically translated into clear, written guidelines for community forums.

base.reply:
Dear friend,

**The number.** I didn't find a numbered position for this passage in what I searched, so I won't guess one. The number in the standard numbering is best read straight from a numbered edition.

**The other book.** I didn't mention [*The Earth Is But One Country*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/john-huddleston_the-earth-is-but-one-country-2) earlier in our conversation, and I found nothing placing this passage there. Its home is [*The Hidden Words*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/core-tablets/bahaullah_the-hidden-words_fa).

**The Golden Rule.** Luke gives it in the positive form: ["And as ye would that men should do to you, do ye also to them likewise"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kjv-gospel-of-luke/?paraId=para_212&selectionString=the-gospel-of-luke_en_8l.0~the-gospel-of-luke_en_8l.56) — [*The Gospel of Luke*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20990). An address in [*The World's Congress of Religions*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/compilations/the-worlds-congress-of-religions-the-addresses-and-papers-delivered-before-the-parliament-and) (1893) sets it beside Confucius's rule, which it calls a negative form, "do not like when done to yourself" ([The World's Congress of Religions: The Addresses and Papers Delivered Before the Parliament, and an Abstract of the Congresses Held in the Art Institute, Chicago, Illinois, U.S.A., August 25 to October 15, 1893](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/compilations/the-worlds-congress-of-religions-the-addresses-and-papers-delivered-before-the-parliament-and#p4718)). A saying in [*Kitab Al-Kafi*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21057) has the Prophet say: ["Do to people what you like them to do to you"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-al-kafi-2/?paraId=para_1848&selectionString=kitab_al_kafi_part_2_ocean_islam_en-bl1vg.0~kitab_al_kafi_part_2_ocean_islam_en-bl1vg.313).

**The Hidden Words.** The reasoning here is different:

> Know ye not why We created you all from the same dust? That no one should exalt himself over the other. … Since We have created you all from one same substance it is incumbent on you to be even as one soul, to walk with the same feet, eat with the same mouth and dwell in the same land, that from your inmost being, by your deeds and actions, the signs of oneness and the essence of detachment may be made manifest. > — Bahá'u'lláh, [*The Hidden Words*](https://oceanlibrary.com/hidden-words-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_212&selectionString=the-hidden-words-prod_en_8n.0~the-hidden-words-prod_en_8n.508)

**Bahá'u'lláh's nearer parallels.** The Golden Rule's own territory is also covered in his Writings. The [*Summons of the Lord of Hosts*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20806) says: ["desire not for anyone the things ye would not desire for yourselves"](https://oceanlibrary.com/summons-of-the-lord-of-hosts_bahaullah/?paraId=para_443&selectionString=summons_of_the_lord_of_hosts_bahai_en-blf1.0~summons_of_the_lord_of_hosts_bahai_en-blf1.160), and calls it "My best counsel". The [*Kitáb-i-Aqdas*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21307) has: ["No one is to approve for another that which he would dislike himself"](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_kitab_aqdas_parallel) — [*The Most Holy Book*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/bahaullah_the-most-holy-book-parallel-translation-of-the-kitab-i-aqdas), parallel translation. These are close to the Confucian, negative form.

**How they differ.** This is my reading. The Golden Rule and the Summons start from yourself. You imagine your own wishes and carry them over to another person. The Hidden Words start from a shared origin. The reason given for not exalting oneself is that all are made of "the same dust", and from that comes "even as one soul". The first is a rule of reciprocity, the second a statement of kinship from which conduct follows. Even so, the Hidden Words don't stay in thought. They ask that oneness appear "by your deeds and actions" ([The Hidden Words of Bahá’u’lláh](https://oceanlibrary.com/hidden-words-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_212&selectionString=the-hidden-words-prod_en_8n.0~the-hidden-words-prod_en_8n.508)), so the ethic is meant to be lived and not only acknowledged. In the Arabic the verb is *yaẓhar*, "to become manifest", and the passage ends by speaking of "fruits of holiness" from a tree.

Seen together, the two kinds of passage might even complete each other: one gives a test you can apply in a moment, the other a ground for why the test works at all. Whether you find that persuasive is for you to weigh.

With warmth,
Anís

claude-haiku-5-5.reply:
Dear friend,

I couldn't confirm the number of the "same dust" passage from what I found. The Arabic text I found opens with this sentence, so it sits at the start of the Arabic [*Hidden Words*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/core-tablets/bahaullah_the-hidden-words_fa). For its number in the standard numbering, check a numbered edition of the Arabic text before you cite it.

I also need to correct my earlier mention of [*The Earth Is But One Country*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/john-huddleston_the-earth-is-but-one-country-2). My search did not support it, and I can't confirm that the "same dust" passage appears in that book, so please set that reference aside.

**The Golden Rule**

The Christian form comes from Luke: ["And as ye would that men should do to you, do ye also to them likewise."](https://oceanlibrary.com/kjv-gospel-of-luke/?paraId=para_212&selectionString=the-gospel-of-luke_en_8l.0~the-gospel-of-luke_en_8l.56) — [*The Gospel of Luke*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20990). In the [*Kitab Al-Kafi*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21057), a companion asks the Prophet for a deed that will bring him to paradise, and the reply is to do to people what one would want done to oneself, and to do nothing to others that one would not want done to oneself ([*Kitab Al-Kafi 2*](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-al-kafi-2/?paraId=para_1848&selectionString=kitab_al_kafi_part_2_ocean_islam_en-bl1vg.0~kitab_al_kafi_part_2_ocean_islam_en-bl1vg.313)). The 1893 [*The World's Congress of Religions*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/compilations/the-worlds-congress-of-religions-the-addresses-and-papers-delivered-before-the-parliament-and) also records Confucius's negative form of the rule, though the scan is hard to read, so I'd check the wording in a clean copy.

**What the Golden Rule does**

Each of these forms works by reciprocity. It takes my own wish as the measure and asks me to imagine myself in another's place. The rule is practical and easy to remember, and it starts from desire.

**What the Hidden Words does**

The "same dust" passage starts somewhere else. It asks: ["Know ye not why We created you all from the same dust? That no one should exalt himself over the other."](https://oceanlibrary.com/hidden-words-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_212&selectionString=the-hidden-words-prod_en_8n.0~the-hidden-words-prod_en_8n.508) — [*The Hidden Words of Bahá'u'lláh*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20809). It then says that, since God has created all from "one same substance," it is incumbent on people "to be even as one soul," ([The Hidden Words of Bahá’u’lláh](https://oceanlibrary.com/hidden-words-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_212&selectionString=the-hidden-words-prod_en_8n.0~the-hidden-words-prod_en_8n.508)) and that this oneness should appear in one's "deeds and actions."

My reading (my own, not a stated teaching) is that the ground moves from what I would want to what we share. The duty is no longer a bargain between two people who might trade places. It is a fact about the human family, and the "one soul" image says that the other person is not a stranger to be measured against oneself.

**Bahá'u'lláh's nearer parallels**

Two other texts of Bahá'u'lláh state the reciprocal form more closely. The Summons says: ["desire not for anyone the things ye would not desire for yourselves."](https://oceanlibrary.com/summons-of-the-lord-of-hosts_bahaullah/?paraId=para_443&selectionString=summons_of_the_lord_of_hosts_bahai_en-blf1.0~summons_of_the_lord_of_hosts_bahai_en-blf1.160) — [*Summons of the Lord of Hosts*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20806). The Kitáb-i-Aqdas, in a parallel translation, says: ["No one is to approve for another that which he would dislike himself."](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_kitab_aqdas_parallel) — [*The Most Holy Book*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/bahaullah_the-most-holy-book-parallel-translation-of-the-kitab-i-aqdas).

So the Summons and the Aqdas give the Golden Rule's form, and the Hidden Words gives its root. I read these as one ethic seen from two sides, though the texts do not put it in those words.

The thread to pull: set the Hidden Words' "same dust" beside the Summons' "desire not for anyone," and ask whether knowing a shared origin changes how the reciprocal rule feels when you use it.

With warmth,
Anís

gemini-3.1-flash-lite.reply:
Hello! It is a pleasure to look into this with you.

Regarding the "same dust" passage, it appears at the very beginning of the Arabic [*Hidden Words*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/core-tablets/bahaullah_the-hidden-words_fa). While many editions number the passages for convenience, the text itself is the primary guide. Because the numbering can vary between different editions and translations, I cannot confirm a specific number for you from the library’s records, but you will find it as the opening passage in the Arabic text.

You asked how this teaching compares to the Golden Rule. The Golden Rule, as found in the Gospel of Luke, is a principle of reciprocity: ["And as ye would that men should do to you, do ye also to them likewise."](https://oceanlibrary.com/kjv-gospel-of-luke/?paraId=para_212&selectionString=the-gospel-of-luke_en_8l.0~the-gospel-of-luke_en_8l.56) [*The Gospel of Luke*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20990). This same reciprocal logic appears in other traditions, such as the Hadith in [*al-Kafi*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21057): ["Do to people what you like them to do to you, and do not do anything to people that you do not like to be done to you."](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-al-kafi-2/?paraId=para_1848&selectionString=kitab_al_kafi_part_2_ocean_islam_en-bl1vg.0~kitab_al_kafi_part_2_ocean_islam_en-bl1vg.313) [*Kitab Al-Kafi 2*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21057).

The *Hidden Words* approaches the matter from a different starting point—not merely how we should act toward one another, but why we are already connected. It grounds our duty in our shared origin:

```bilingual
هَلْ عَرَفْتُمْ لِمَ خَلَقْناكُمْ مِنْ تُرابٍ واحِدٍ؛
Know ye not why We created you all from the same dust? <sup>1</sup>
لِئَلاَّ يَفْتَخِرَ أَحَدٌ عَلى أَحَدٍ.
That no one should exalt himself over the other. <sup>1</sup>
إِذاً يَنْبَغِي كَما خَلَقْناكُم مِنْ شَيْءٍ واحِدٍ أَنْ تَكُونُوا كَنَفْسٍ واحِدَةٍ
Since We have created you all from one same substance it is incumbent on you to be even as one soul <sup>1</sup>
```
<sup>1</sup> [*The Hidden Words of Bahá’u’lláh*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20809)

While the Golden Rule asks us to consider the other as we consider ourselves, this passage suggests that we are, in essence, already "one soul." The duty to act with kindness is not just a social contract, but a reflection of a pre-existing reality.

Bahá’u’lláh does provide counsel that mirrors the Golden Rule, such as in [*The Summons of the Lord of Hosts*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20806): ["desire not for anyone the things ye would not desire for yourselves. This is My best counsel unto you"](https://oceanlibrary.com/summons-of-the-lord-of-hosts_bahaullah/?paraId=para_443&selectionString=summons_of_the_lord_of_hosts_bahai_en-blf1.0~summons_of_the_lord_of_hosts_bahai_en-blf1.160) *The Summons of the Lord of Hosts*. Similarly, in the [*Kitáb-i-Aqdas*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21307), it is written: ["No one is to approve for another that which he would dislike himself."](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_kitab_aqdas_parallel) [*The Most Holy Book*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/tablet-translations/bahaullah_the-most-holy-book-parallel-translation-of-the-kitab-i-aqdas).

It seems to me that the "same dust" passage provides the ontological foundation—the *why*—for the practical counsel of the Golden Rule. If we are created from the same substance, then the Golden Rule is not just a helpful social strategy, but a necessary expression of our own nature.

I hope this helps you see the distinction between the two ways of framing this ethic. You might find it interesting to compare the "same dust" passage with the counsel in *The Summons of the Lord of Hosts* to see how the same moral outcome is reached through different paths: one through the recognition of our shared origin, and the other through the application of reciprocal restraint.

<sup>1</sup> Authorized translation by Shoghi Effendi, [*The Hidden Words of Bahá’u’lláh*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20809)

The Golden Rule is a familiar threshold across traditions. In the New Testament, Luke records: [“And as ye would that men should do to you, do ye also to them likewise.”](https://oceanlibrary.com/kjv-gospel-of-luke/?paraId=para_212&selectionString=the-gospel-of-luke_en_8l.0~the-gospel-of-luke_en_8l.56) ([*The Bible (KJV), The Gospel of Luke*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=912528)) ([The Bible (KJV), The Gospel of Luke](https://oceanlibrary.com/kjv-gospel-of-luke/?paraId=para_212&selectionString=the-gospel-of-luke_en_8l.0~the-gospel-of-luke_en_8l.56)). In Islamic tradition, al-Kulayni records the Prophet Muhammad advising an Arab traveler: [“Do to people what you like them to do to you, and do not do anything to people that you do not like to be done to you.”](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-al-kafi-2/?paraId=para_1848&selectionString=kitab_al_kafi_part_2_ocean_islam_en-bl1vg.0~kitab_al_kafi_part_2_ocean_islam_en-bl1vg.313) ([*Kitab Al-Kafi 2*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21057)) ([Kitab Al-Kafi 2](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-al-kafi-2/?paraId=para_1848&selectionString=kitab_al_kafi_part_2_ocean_islam_en-bl1vg.0~kitab_al_kafi_part_2_ocean_islam_en-bl1vg.313)).

Bahá'u'lláh expresses a similar ethic in [*The Summons of the Lord of Hosts*](https://oceanlibrary.com/summons-of-the-lord-of-hosts_bahaullah/?paraId=para_443&selectionString=summons_of_the_lord_of_hosts_bahai_en-blf1.0~summons_of_the_lord_of_hosts_bahai_en-blf1.160):

This is My best counsel unto you, did ye but observe it.](https://oceanlibrary.com/summons-of-the-lord-of-hosts_bahaullah/?paraId=para_443&selectionString=summons_of_the_lord_of_hosts_bahai_en-blf1.0~summons_of_the_lord_of_hosts_bahai_en-blf1.160) ([*Summons of the Lord of Hosts*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20806)) ([Summons of the Lord of Hosts](https://oceanlibrary.com/summons-of-the-lord-of-hosts_bahaullah/?paraId=para_443&selectionString=summons_of_the_lord_of_hosts_bahai_en-blf1.0~summons_of_the_lord_of_hosts_bahai_en-blf1.160))

A parallel rendering appears in [*The Most Holy Book: Parallel Translation of the Kitáb-i-Aqdas*](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_kitab_aqdas_parallel): ["No one is to approve for another that which he would dislike himself."](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_kitab_aqdas_parallel) ([The Most Holy Book: Parallel Translation of the Kitáb-i-Aqdas](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_kitab_aqdas_parallel)).

The difference between these formulations and the opening of *The Hidden Words* lies in where the duty is anchored. The Golden Rule operates through reciprocity—treating others as one wishes to be treated. The Hidden Words ground human relationship in a shared ontological origin. Warmly,
Anís
