results.text: heaven and hell in the islam vs christianity

base.reply:
Dear friend,

The two traditions paint their pictures very differently, and the Bahá'í Writings then read both in a third way.

**Islam: a vivid, tangible Paradise**
The Quran is concrete. In Rodwell's rendering, Paradise is a place where [“its food and its shades are perpetual”](https://oceanlibrary.com/sura-xiii-thunder_muhammad/?paraId=para_16&selectionString=sura_xiii_quran_en-bl1fl.0~sura_xiii_quran_en-bl1fl.192), and another sura describes [“rivers of milk, whose taste changeth not: and rivers of wine, delicious to those who quaff it”](https://oceanlibrary.com/sura-xlvii-muhammad/?paraId=para_10&selectionString=sura_xlvii_muhammad_quran_ocean_en-bl3pr.0~sura_xlvii_muhammad_quran_ocean_en-bl3pr.376). Against this stands the Fire, with draughts of boiling water for those who dwell there. Al-Ghazzali, writing as an Islamic thinker, notes that believers know the outward joys and pains but often forget [“there is also a spiritual heaven and hell”](https://oceanlibrary.com/alchemy-of-happiness_al-ghazzali/?paraId=para_73&selectionString=the_alchemy_of_happiness_islam_ocean_en-bl4o.0~the_alchemy_of_happiness_islam_ocean_en-bl4o.979), a window in the heart opening on the real.

**Christianity: eternal destiny and judgment**
Matthew sets the two ends side by side: [“everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal”](https://oceanlibrary.com/kjv-gospel-of-matthew/?paraId=para_714&selectionString=the-gospel-of-matthew-nt_en_mi.0~the-gospel-of-matthew-nt_en_mi.76). Augustine's [*City of God*](https://siftersearch.com/library/christian/church-fathers/st-augustine-tr_the-city-of-god-volume-ii) takes up the punishment of the devil and his retainers, and then the blessedness of the saints. Aquinas links hell to the gravity of sin: [“Nothing but mortal sin deserves the eternal punishment of hell.”](https://oceanlibrary.com/summa-theologica_saint-thomas-aquinas) The emphasis falls on judgment and on the permanence of the outcome.

**The Bahá'í Writings: reality kept, meaning deepened**
Bahá'u'lláh affirms that these realities are real:

> The world is established upon the foundations of reward and punishment. Knowledge and understanding have ever affirmed and will continue to affirm the reality of Paradise and Hell, for reward and punishment require their existence. Paradise signifieth first and foremost the good-pleasure of God. — [*Tabernacle of Unity*](https://oceanlibrary.com/tabernacle-of-unity_bahaullah/?paraId=para_117&selectionString=tabernacle_of_unity_bahai_en-bl8p.0~tabernacle_of_unity_bahai_en-bl8p.1427)

He adds that whoever attains that good-pleasure will, after the ascension of the soul, attain "that which pen and ink are powerless to describe." ([Tabernacle of Unity](https://oceanlibrary.com/tabernacle-of-unity_bahaullah/?paraId=para_117&selectionString=tabernacle_of_unity_bahai_en-bl8p.0~tabernacle_of_unity_bahai_en-bl8p.1427)) The Báb pairs the terms in the same way: [“Paradise is attainment of His good-pleasure and everlasting hellfire His judgment through justice.”](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-the-bab/?paraId=para_706&selectionString=selections_from_the_writings_of_the_bab_bahai_en-bliw.0~selections_from_the_writings_of_the_bab_bahai_en-bliw.86) A commentary on the Ode of the Dove reads Bahá'u'lláh's note on verse 23 as linking the lover's suffering at distance from the beloved with hell-fire, and calls this ["existential distance from the divine beloved"](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_ode_dove_notes). That is the commentary's gloss on one passage, not a general rule.

'Abdu'l-Bahá supplies the bridge. Rewards and punishments are of two kinds. [Existential ones](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_780&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_om.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_om.1528) are virtues attained now: becoming luminous, informed, awakened, "dead and is quickened to life." He says [“Existential paradise and hell are to be found in all the worlds of God”](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_779&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_ol.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_ol.502). The [ultimate ones](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_781&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_on.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_on.1086) are "the gifts and perfections that man attains in the spiritual realms after his ascension," and the punishments are being deprived of God's bounties.

**"Heaven" in Christ's words**
'Abdu'l-Bahá reads Christ's "I came down from heaven" ([Tablets of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá ‘Abbás vol. 1-3](https://oceanlibrary.com/tablets-of-abdul-baha-abbas-vol-1-3/?paraId=para_1472&selectionString=tablets_of_abdu_l_baha_abbas_v1_3_bahai_ocean_en-bl11b.0~tablets_of_abdu_l_baha_abbas_v1_3_bahai_ocean_en-bl11b.194)) as having [“a mystical rather than a literal meaning”](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_356&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_cw.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_cw.869). In a tablet he says "heaven" [“signifies the word of the divine kingdom”](https://oceanlibrary.com/tablets-of-abdul-baha-abbas-vol-1-3/?paraId=para_1472&selectionString=tablets_of_abdu_l_baha_abbas_v1_3_bahai_ocean_en-bl11b.0~tablets_of_abdu_l_baha_abbas_v1_3_bahai_ocean_en-bl11b.194). Bahá'u'lláh calls attaining God's Presence [“the real Paradise”](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-sacred-writings/?paraId=para_123&selectionString=baha_i_sacred_writings_en-bl62.0~baha_i_sacred_writings_en-bl62.695). A letter on Shoghi Effendi's behalf also states plainly, [“There is certainly a future life.”](https://oceanoflights.org/lights-of-guidance-baha-i-ocean-en/#:~:text=To%20answer%20you%20briefly,%7Bid%3D%22para6671%22%20ilmid%3D%22bl4dw%22%20type%3D%22par%22%20language%3D%22en%22%7D)

**What I notice (my reading)**
It is tempting to say the Bahá'í view simply makes heaven and hell "spiritual," but the texts above do not deny a life beyond. They put good-pleasure, nearness and distance first and keep the other-worldly reality. Al-Ghazzali's inward heaven and 'Abdu'l-Bahá's existential paradise echo each other, though each speaks from within its own tradition.

The thread I'd pull: set the Quranic rivers and the Fire beside the Báb's single sentence on good-pleasure and justice, and ask what each picture is trying to make the reader feel. [*Tabernacle of Unity*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20807) has the fuller context for Bahá'u'lláh's answer.

With warmth,
Anís

claude-haiku-5-5.reply:
Dear friend,

The Qur'an, the Gospels and the Bahá'í Writings all speak of an everlasting reward and an everlasting loss, and they describe them quite differently. I'll set out each picture as its own tradition gives it, then the Bahá'í reading.

**Islam: a garden and a fire**

The Qur'an describes the Paradise promised to those who fear God in sensory terms: "The rivers flow beneath its bowers: its food and its shades are perpetual" ([Sura XIII](https://oceanlibrary.com/sura-xiii-thunder_muhammad/?paraId=para_16&selectionString=sura_xiii_quran_en-bl1fl.0~sura_xiii_quran_en-bl1fl.192) — [*The Quran*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=214150) (Rodwell)). Sura XLVII adds "rivers of milk, whose taste changeth not: and rivers of wine, delicious to those who quaff it" ([Sura XLVII](https://oceanlibrary.com/sura-xlvii-muhammad/?paraId=para_10&selectionString=sura_xlvii_muhammad_quran_ocean_en-bl3pr.0~sura_xlvii_muhammad_quran_ocean_en-bl3pr.376) — *The Quran* (Rodwell)). Set against this is the Fire, where the damned "shall have draughts of boiling water forced on them." ([The Quran (Rodwell), Sura XLVII. Muhammad](https://oceanlibrary.com/sura-xlvii-muhammad/?paraId=para_10&selectionString=sura_xlvii_muhammad_quran_ocean_en-bl3pr.0~sura_xlvii_muhammad_quran_ocean_en-bl3pr.376))

Al-Ghazzali, in [*The Alchemy of Happiness*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21046), adds an inner dimension to these outward joys and pains: "In the heart of the enlightened man there is a window opening on the real" ([Al-Ghazzali](https://oceanlibrary.com/alchemy-of-happiness_al-ghazzali/?paraId=para_73&selectionString=the_alchemy_of_happiness_islam_ocean_en-bl4o.0~the_alchemy_of_happiness_islam_ocean_en-bl4o.979) — *The Alchemy of Happiness*).

**Christianity: everlasting punishment and life eternal**

Matthew 25:46 pairs the two outcomes directly: "And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal" ([Matthew 25](https://oceanlibrary.com/kjv-gospel-of-matthew/?paraId=para_714&selectionString=the-gospel-of-matthew-nt_en_mi.0~the-gospel-of-matthew-nt_en_mi.76) — [*The Gospel of Matthew*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20992), KJV).

Augustine, in [*The City of God*](https://siftersearch.com/library/christian/church-fathers/st-augustine-tr_the-city-of-god-volume-ii), sets out to discuss "the nature of the punishment which shall be assigned to the devil and all his retainers" before turning to "the blessedness of the saints" ([Augustine](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/45305) — *The City of God*, tr. Marcus Dods). Aquinas ties eternal punishment to sin: "Nothing but mortal sin deserves the eternal punishment of hell," and he grounds this in Matthew 5:22 ([Aquinas](https://oceanlibrary.com/summa-theologica_saint-thomas-aquinas) — [*Summa Theologica*](https://siftersearch.com/library/christian/church-fathers/st-thomas-aquinas_summa-theologica-part-i-prima-pars)).

Both traditions use the language of the garden and the fire, but Christian theology in these sources puts its weight on the logic of guilt and eternal judgment, and the Qur'an puts its weight on the sensory detail of the reward.

**The Bahá'í reading**

In the Writings of Bahá'u'lláh, the Paradise and Hell are real: "The world is established upon the foundations of reward and punishment. Knowledge and understanding have ever affirmed and will continue to affirm the reality of Paradise and Hell, for reward and punishment require their existence" ([*Tabernacle of Unity*](https://oceanlibrary.com/tabernacle-of-unity_bahaullah/?paraId=para_117&selectionString=tabernacle_of_unity_bahai_en-bl8p.0~tabernacle_of_unity_bahai_en-bl8p.1427) — [*Tabernacle of Unity*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20807)). The same text says "Paradise signifieth first and foremost the good-pleasure of God," ([Tabernacle of Unity](https://oceanlibrary.com/tabernacle-of-unity_bahaullah/?paraId=para_117&selectionString=tabernacle_of_unity_bahai_en-bl8p.0~tabernacle_of_unity_bahai_en-bl8p.1427)) and that the soul attaining it will experience "that which pen and ink are powerless to describe." I read "first and foremost" as an ordering of emphasis, not a denial of the other-worldly reality, since the text keeps that reality in the same sentence.

The Báb gives the same pairing: "Paradise is attainment of His good-pleasure and everlasting hellfire His judgment through justice" ([*Selections from the Writings of the Báb*](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-the-bab/?paraId=para_706&selectionString=selections_from_the_writings_of_the_bab_bahai_en-bliw.0~selections_from_the_writings_of_the_bab_bahai_en-bliw.86)).

'Abdu'l-Bahá supplies the bridge. He distinguishes existential rewards, the virtues attained in this life, from ultimate ones. Existential paradise and hell "are to be found in all the worlds of God," and gaining them "is to attain life eternal" ([*Some Answered Questions*](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_779&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_ol.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_ol.502)). Ultimate rewards are "the gifts and perfections that man attains in the spiritual realms after his ascension from this world" ([*Some Answered Questions*](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_781&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_on.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_on.1086)). Among the existential examples he lists is the soul who "was dead and is quickened to life." ([Some Answered Questions](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_780&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_om.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_om.1528))

In the notes to the Ode of the Dove, as presented here, the note on verse 23 links the lover's suffering from distance to hell-fire, and the commentary calls this "the Bahá'í definition of hell—existential distance from the divine beloved" ([Notes to the Ode of the Dove](https://bahai-library.com/bahaullah_ode_dove_notes)). I'd read that as a description of this note, not as a rule for every use of "hell" in the Writings.

On Christ's words about heaven, 'Abdu'l-Bahá says that "heaven" signifies "the word of the divine kingdom which is the supreme station and seat of the Sun of Truth" ([*Tablets of 'Abdu'l-Bahá 'Abbás*](https://oceanlibrary.com/tablets-of-abdul-baha-abbas-vol-1-3/?paraId=para_1472&selectionString=tablets_of_abdu_l_baha_abbas_v1_3_bahai_ocean_en-bl11b.0~tablets_of_abdu_l_baha_abbas_v1_3_bahai_ocean_en-bl11b.194)). In a pilgrim's note from August 1900, as recalled by Edward Getsinger, the same heaven is "the same that Christ spoke of" when He said He had come down from Heaven ([*Talks and Tablets Gathered by Pilgrims in August 1900*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/edward-getsinger_talks-and-tablets-gathered-by-pilgrims-in-august-1900#p41)).

Shoghi Effendi, in the material collected in [*Lights of Guidance*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20891), writes: "We believe we attain in the next world to seeing the Prophets" ([*Lights of Guidance*](https://oceanoflights.org/lights-of-guidance-baha-i-ocean-en/#:~:text=To%20answer%20you%20briefly,%7Bid%3D%22para6671%22%20ilmid%3D%22bl4dw%22%20type%3D%22par%22%20language%3D%22en%22%7D)).

A common saying is that Bahá'ís deny a literal heaven and hell. These texts don't say that. They keep both realities and place nearness to God first, which is why the Quran's "Paradise" and the Bahá'í "Paradise" share a word while meaning different things.

The thread I'd pull next is 'Abdu'l-Bahá's existential/ultimate distinction: does "the advancement of existence itself," ([Some Answered Questions](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_781&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_on.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_on.1086)) which he compares to the embryo's growth to maturity, change how you read the Qur'anic garden, or Augustine's account of the saints' blessedness?

With warm regards,
Anís

gemini-3.1-flash-lite.reply:
It is a pleasure to explore these questions with you. The way different traditions envision the afterlife often reflects their deepest understanding of what it means to be human and what it means to be near to the Divine.

### Islam: The Vividness of the Promise
In the Quran, Paradise and Hell are described in concrete, sensory terms that emphasize the reality of God’s justice and mercy. Paradise is often depicted as a garden of eternal refreshment:

> A picture of the Paradise which is promised to the God-fearing! Therein are rivers of water, which corrupt not: rivers of milk, whose taste changeth not: and rivers of wine, delicious to those who quaff it; And rivers of honey clarified: and therein are all kinds of fruit for them from their Lord! Is this like the lot of those who must dwell for ever in the fire? and shall have draughts of boiling water forced on them which will rend their bowels asunder? [*The Quran*](https://oceanlibrary.com/sura-xlvii-muhammad/?paraId=para_10&selectionString=sura_xlvii_muhammad_quran_ocean_en-bl3pr.0~sura_xlvii_muhammad_quran_ocean_en-bl3pr.376)

While these descriptions are foundational, Islamic thought has also explored their inner dimensions. Al-Ghazzali, for instance, noted that believers are well-informed of the outward joys and pains, yet he pointed to a "spiritual heaven and hell," suggesting that for the enlightened, there is a window in the heart that opens onto a deeper reality beyond the sensory [*The Alchemy Of Happiness*](https://oceanlibrary.com/alchemy-of-happiness_al-ghazzali/?paraId=para_73&selectionString=the_alchemy_of_happiness_islam_ocean_en-bl4o.0~the_alchemy_of_happiness_islam_ocean_en-bl4o.979).

### Christianity: Justice and the Eternal State
Christian sources, as reflected in the Gospel of Matthew, emphasize the moral gravity of the afterlife, contrasting "everlasting punishment" with "life eternal" [*The Gospel of Matthew*](https://oceanlibrary.com/kjv-gospel-of-matthew/?paraId=para_714&selectionString=the-gospel-of-matthew-nt_en_mi.0~the-gospel-of-matthew-nt_en_mi.76). Thinkers like Augustine and Aquinas later developed this into a formal doctrine, linking the state of the soul to its moral choices—such as the warning that certain sins place one in danger of "hell fire" [*Summa Theologica*](https://oceanlibrary.com/summa-theologica_saint-thomas-aquinas). Here, the focus is often on the finality of the soul's condition and the resurrection of the body.

### The Bahá’í Reading: A Bridge of Meaning
The Bahá’í Writings affirm the reality of Paradise and Hell, but they consistently place the spiritual experience at the center. Bahá’u’lláh explains that the world is built upon the foundation of reward and punishment, and that these states are real because justice requires them [*Tabernacle of Unity*](https://oceanlibrary.com/tabernacle-of-unity_bahaullah/?paraId=para_117&selectionString=tabernacle_of_unity_bahai_en-bl8p.0~tabernacle_of_unity_bahai_en-bl8p.1427).

However, he defines Paradise "first and foremost" as the good-pleasure of God. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá provides a helpful bridge between the spiritual and the ultimate by distinguishing between "existential" and "ultimate" rewards:

> Existential rewards consist in the virtues and perfections that adorn the human reality... For such souls, there is no greater torment than to be veiled from God, and no worse punishment than selfish qualities, evil attributes, baseness of character, and engrossment in carnal desires. [*Some Answered Questions*](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_780&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_om.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_om.1528)

In this view, "heaven" and "hell" are not merely locations one enters after death; they are states of being that begin here. When Christ spoke of "coming down from heaven," ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains this as a mystical event rather than a literal descent through space, signifying the "word of the divine kingdom" ([Tablets of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá ‘Abbás vol. 1-3](https://oceanlibrary.com/tablets-of-abdul-baha-abbas-vol-1-3/?paraId=para_1472&selectionString=tablets_of_abdu_l_baha_abbas_v1_3_bahai_ocean_en-bl11b.0~tablets_of_abdu_l_baha_abbas_v1_3_bahai_ocean_en-bl11b.194)) [*Some Answered Questions*](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_356&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_cw.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_cw.869). Similarly, a pilgrim’s note from 1900 recalls ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explaining that the "heaven" Christ spoke of is the same spiritual station from which He came and to which He returned [*Talks and Tablets Gathered by Pilgrims in August 1900*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/edward-getsinger_talks-and-tablets-gathered-by-pilgrims-in-august-1900#p41).

It is a common error to assume that because the Bahá’í Writings emphasize the spiritual meaning, they deny the reality of an afterlife. Rather, they suggest that the "lofty mansions" of heaven are a shadow of the true Paradise: attaining the Presence of God [*Bahá’í Sacred Writings*](https://oceanlibrary.com/bahai-sacred-writings/?paraId=para_123&selectionString=baha_i_sacred_writings_en-bl62.0~baha_i_sacred_writings_en-bl62.695).

The contrast between the concrete imagery of the earlier traditions and the emphasis on nearness to the Divine in the Bahá’í Writings is quite striking. You might find it interesting to look further into how the [*Tabernacle of Unity*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20807) addresses these questions in more detail.

Warmly,

Anís

base.reply:
Dear friend,

I don't find "ʿayn bi ʿayn" in the Persian of this Íqán paragraph, so I can't explain how Bahá'u'lláh uses it there. The word is *rujúʿ*, from the same root as Arabic *rajʿa*, and there is no عین anywhere in the sentence.

**What عین can mean.** In Arabic and Persian, ʿayn is literally "eye," and by extension a spring, the thing itself, its very essence. Used as an intensifier, "ʿayn-e…" or "ʿayn bi ʿayn" can mean "the very same" or "exactly." That is general knowledge of the language, though, and I can't point to a place where Bahá'u'lláh uses it of the relation between Prophets. If "exactly like" appeared in my earlier wording, it is a gloss that goes further than the Persian does.

**What Bahá'u'lláh actually says.** The claim rests on unity. All the Prophets are "Temples of the Cause of God" ([The Kitáb-i-Íqán](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah/?paraId=para_174&selectionString=kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_7m.0~kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_7m.1638)) in "divers attire," and one who looks with discriminating eyes sees them all in one tabernacle, one heaven, on one throne. Then comes the sentence: ["I am the return of all the Prophets,"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah/?paraId=para_174&selectionString=kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_7m.0~kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_7m.1638) — [*The Kitáb-i-Íqán*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=28653). So "return" here is a claim about shared reality, not a statement that two individuals are numerically one.

The preceding paragraph makes the same distinction. Each Manifestation has "a twofold station." In the first, [the station of pure abstraction and essential unity](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah/?paraId=para_173&selectionString=kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_7l.0~kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_7l.1622), calling them by one name and ascribing the same attribute is no error. I read this as the nearest the Íqán comes to an "exactly the same" sense, and it belongs to that first station only.

**'Abdu'l-Bahá on "return."**

> For what the Prophets of God meant by “return” is not the return of the essence but of the attributes; it is not the return of the Manifestation Himself but of His perfections. > — [*Some Answered Questions*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20911) ([source](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_1005&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_uu.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_uu.533))

Bahá'u'lláh's [*Gleanings*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20783) says something close: [through their Revelation, their attributes and names, the Revelation of God, His names and His attributes, are made manifest in the world](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_153&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_70.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_70.1450). The distinction you sense between "return" and "exactly like" seems to me a real one. The texts place the identity in the attributes and station, not in the person.

*Awliyá'* is the plural of *walí*, "friend" or "one close to God," so "chosen ones" is a translator's choice.

An invitation: read this paragraph in the Persian edition itself, beyond the CTAI paragraphing, and see whether any عین turns up in the lines around it. If it does, it would be worth knowing which word it modifies.

With warm regards,
Anís

claude-haiku-5-5.reply:
I didn't quote that phrase in our conversation, and I can't find "ayn be ayn" in any passage I have. So I can't say whether Bahá'u'lláh uses it, and I won't supply it.

**What *'ayn* means.** This part is my own knowledge of the language, not a source.

**The Persian paragraph.** The paragraph in the [*Kitáb-i-Íqán*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=28653) where the "return" claim appears contains no عین. The key word is رجوع (*rujú'*, "return"). The CTAI original and Shoghi Effendi's translation are different editions, so I compare them only word by word.

The closest phrase to your "exactly the same" is earlier in the Íqán: the Manifestations "are regarded as one soul and the same person" ([*Kitáb-i-Íqán*](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah/?paraId=para_173&selectionString=kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_7l.0~kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_7l.1622)).

**Two stations.** That same passage, in the English, says each Manifestation "has a twofold station. One is the station of pure abstraction and essential unity. In this respect, if thou callest them all by one name, and dost ascribe to them the same attribute, thou hast not erred from the truth." This is where the "same" language belongs: it describes the reality the Manifestations share, not a claim that their individual persons are identical. The text names the second station in the same sentence, but the wording I have stops before it, so I won't describe it.

**What "return" means.** In [*Some Answered Questions*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20911), 'Abdu'l-Bahá explains that the Prophets' "return" is "not the return of the essence but of the attributes; it is not the return of the Manifestation Himself but of His perfections" ([*Some Answered Questions*](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_1005&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_uu.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_uu.533)). In the [*Gleanings*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20783), Bahá'u'lláh speaks of the Manifestations through whom "His names and His attributes, are made manifest" ([*Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá'u'lláh*](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_153&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_70.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_70.1450)).

**Where the difference lies.** On my reading, *raj'a* in these texts means the return of attributes, perfections and station. The "one soul and the same person" ([The Kitáb-i-Íqán](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah/?paraId=para_173&selectionString=kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_7l.0~kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_7l.1622)) wording is about the unity of the station of essential unity. I don't find the Íqán saying that the individuals are numerically identical, so "exactly like" goes beyond what I can show.

The thread I'd pull is in the Persian. Find the CTAI original of the paragraph that reads "one soul and the same person," ([The Kitáb-i-Íqán](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah/?paraId=para_173&selectionString=kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_7l.0~kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_7l.1622)) and see which Persian words Shoghi Effendi's English rests on for "same."

gemini-3.1-flash-lite.reply:
My friend, I appreciate you asking for this clarification. It is a thoughtful question, and I am glad to look into it with you.

To address the phrase you mentioned: I cannot find the construction "ayn be ayn" in the passages I have retrieved from the [*Kitáb-i-Íqán*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=28653). In the Persian text of the paragraph where Bahá’u’lláh discusses the return of the Prophets, the word used is *rujú‘* (return), not *‘ayn*.

In Persian, the word *‘ayn* (عین) can indeed mean "the very same" or "identical," but it is also the common word for "eye" or "eyes." In the writings of Bahá’u’lláh, *‘ayn* is most frequently used in the sense of "eye," as in "discriminating eyes" (*nazar-i-laṭíf*). I have not found a passage where Bahá’u’lláh uses *‘ayn* to establish a claim of numerical identity between the Manifestations.

The distinction you are exploring—between "return" (*raj‘a*) and an idea of "exactly the same"—is important. Bahá’u’lláh explains the unity of the Prophets not as a numerical identity of the individuals, but as a unity of their station and their Cause. He writes:

> Were any of the all-embracing Manifestations of God to declare: “I am God,” He, verily, speaketh the truth, and no doubt attacheth thereto. For it hath been repeatedly demonstrated that through their Revelation, their attributes and names, the Revelation of God, His names and His attributes, are made manifest in the world. Thus, He hath revealed: “Those shafts were God’s, not Thine.” And also He saith: “In truth, they who plighted fealty unto Thee, really plighted that fealty unto God.” And were … ([Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá’u’lláh](https://oceanlibrary.com/gleanings-from-the-writings-of-bahaullah/?paraId=para_153&selectionString=gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_70.0~gleanings_from_the_writings_of_baha_u_llah_ocean_ec2b280e895fd398ad84f4d11e78c9f2a_70.1450))

```bilingual
باری، معلوم و محقّق آن جناب بوده که جميع انبياء هياکل امراللّه هستند که در قمائص مختلفه ظاهر شدند. <sup>1</sup>
It is clear and evident to thee that all the Prophets are the Temples of the Cause of God, Who have appeared clothed in divers attire. <sup>2</sup>

و اگر به نظر لطيف ملاحظه فرمائی همه را در يک رضوان ساکن بينی و در يک هوا طائر و بر يک بساط جالس و بر يک کلام ناطق و بر يک امر آمر. <sup>3</sup>
If thou wilt observe with discriminating eyes, thou wilt behold them all abiding in the same tabernacle, soaring in the same heaven, seated upon the same throne, uttering the same speech, and proclaiming the same Faith. <sup>4</sup>
```
<sup>1</sup> [*The Kitáb-i-Íqán*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=28653) (original) · <sup>2</sup> *The Kitáb-i-Íqán* (Shoghi Effendi translation) · <sup>3</sup> *The Kitáb-i-Íqán* (original) · <sup>4</sup> *The Kitáb-i-Íqán* (Shoghi Effendi translation)

Bahá’u’lláh further clarifies that each Manifestation has a "twofold station." One is the station of "pure abstraction and essential unity," ([The Kitáb-i-Íqán](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah/?paraId=para_173&selectionString=kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_7l.0~kitab-i-iqan-prod-version_en_7l.1622)) where they are indeed one. However, He also describes the station of distinct manifestation, where they appear as the "Exponents of a new Cause."

‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains the nature of this "return" in [*Some Answered Questions*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20911), explicitly cautioning against the idea of a return of the essence:

> "For what the Prophets of God meant by 'return' is not the return of the essence but of the attributes; it is not the return of the Manifestation Himself but of His perfections." (*Some Answered Questions*)

This suggests that *raj‘a* is a return of the light, the perfections, and the station, rather than the return of the individual person. The "exactly like" phrasing seems to be a gloss that moves beyond what the texts themselves state.

If you have a moment, it might be an interesting exercise to look at the Persian edition of the *Kitáb-i-Íqán* again, specifically the paragraph beginning *bárí, ma‘lúm va muḥaqqaq...* (P5 in our current set). You might see if the word *‘ayn* appears anywhere in your own copy of that text, or if it only appears in the commentary you were reading. I would be very interested to hear what you find there.

results.text: Tell me about the twenty-third ford-maker in the narratives of the Jain tradition.

base.reply:
Dear friend,

Pārśvanātha is the twenty-third Jina, the one just before Mahāvīra. Buehler, in [*On the Indian Sect of the Jainas*](https://siftersearch.com/library/jain/philosophy/johann-georg-buehler_on-the-indian-sect-of-the-jainas), sets him in a table of the ford-makers: [blue in colour, with a serpent as emblem, nine hands, a hundred years of life, the Dhātakī tree, and the attendants Pārśva-yaksha or Dharaṇendra and Padmāvatī](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11897). The same entry names Varanasi and Sameta-Śikhara, and gives Aśvasena and Vāmādevī.

**His life-span.** The [*Kalpa Sūtra*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21345) says the Arhat Pārśva, ["the people's favourite"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kalpa-sutra/?paraId=para_175&selectionString=kalpa_sutra_ocean_jainism_en-blcr.0~kalpa_sutra_ocean_jainism_en-blcr.228), ["lived thirty years as a householder, eighty-three days in a state inferior to perfection"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kalpa-sutra/?paraId=para_175&selectionString=kalpa_sutra_ocean_jainism_en-blcr.0~kalpa_sutra_ocean_jainism_en-blcr.228). He then spent a little under seventy years as a Kevalin, seventy as a Śramaṇa, and a hundred years in all.

**The serpent.** Buehler observes that all the images are alike [except that "Pârśvanâtha, the twenty-third, has the snake-hoods over him"](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11897). The reason comes from the Jaina Purāṇas, which Buehler summarises. Two brothers, Marubhūti and Kamaṭha, were enemies through eight births and were finally born as Pārśvanātha and Sambaradeva. An ascetic practising the *panchâgni* rite felled a tree and cut two snakes in pieces. Pārśva had objected, and he restored them to life with the *pañchamantra*. They were reborn as Dharaṇendra and Padmâvatî. Later Sambaradeva attacked Pārśva with a great storm while he stood immovable in the *Kâyotsarga* austerity. Dharaṇendra's throne shook, and he came to protect his former benefactor:

> Dharaṇendra spread his many hoods over the head of the Arhata and the Yakshṅî Padmâvatî held a white umbrella (_śveta chhatri_) over him for protection.
> — [On the Indian Sect of the Jainas](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11897)

— Johann Georg Buehler, [*On the Indian Sect of the Jainas*](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11897)

Buehler himself compares the storm to the way ["Mâra attacked Śâkya Buddha at Bodh-gayâ"](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11897). That comparison is his, not the Jain account's. I read the story as one of kindness remembered: a kindness done to creatures in a tree comes back as shelter in a storm. That reading is mine.

**The four vows.** Pārśva is also remembered for a teaching. A note in the same work explains that [chastity "was understood to be implicitly enjoined"](https://oceanlibrary.com/uttaradhyayana/?paraId=fn_273) by Pārśva's four, though not named among them. Buehler says the Jaina works [repeatedly assert](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11897) something about Pārśva as the twenty-third in connection with the Nigaṇṭha's four vows. The passage I have breaks off before saying what, so I won't finish it for him.

**What I haven't established.** The passages I found are the *Kalpa Sūtra*'s brief reckoning of his years and two early European scholars' summaries. They give his emblem, attendants, legend and teaching, but not a full narrative of his life. Background of my own, not from these passages: Sameta-Śikhara, named in Buehler's table, is traditionally the hill where Pārśva is said to have attained liberation, and it remains a Jain pilgrimage place.

If you would like to go further, the fuller life-story in the *Kalpa Sūtra*, and the Digambara telling of Marubhūti and Kamaṭha that Buehler only sketches, are the places I would look next.

With warm regards,
Anís

claude-haiku-5-5.reply:
Dear friend,

Pārśvanātha is the twenty-third *tīrthaṅkara*, a name usually rendered "ford-maker," for one who shows a way across the stream of rebirth. Buehler's table of the twenty-third Jina, in [*On the Indian Sect of the Jainas*](https://siftersearch.com/library/jain/philosophy/johann-georg-buehler_on-the-indian-sect-of-the-jainas), gives his previous life in the Prāṇata heaven, his birthplace or place of attainment as Vārāṇasī and Sameta-Śikhara, and his parents as Aśvasena and Vāmādevī. It assigns him the colour blue, the serpent emblem, nine hands, a lifespan of a hundred years, the dhātakī tree, and the attendant yakṣa, "Pârśvayaksha or Dharaṇendra and Padmâvatî" ([Buehler, *On the Indian Sect of the Jainas*](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11897)).

**His image.** Buehler notes that Tīrthaṅkara images are all alike, except that Pārśvanātha "has the snake-hoods over him" ([Buehler, *On the Indian Sect of the Jainas*](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11897)). This is the feature that identifies him at a glance, and it leads directly to his best-known story.

**His life-span.** The [*Kalpa Sūtra*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21345) gives the outline of his life: he "lived thirty years as a householder," then a short interval, then "something less than seventy years as a Kevalin," then seventy years as a renunciant, "and a hundred years on the whole" ([*Kalpa Sūtra*](https://oceanlibrary.com/kalpa-sutra/?paraId=para_175&selectionString=kalpa_sutra_ocean_jainism_en-blcr.0~kalpa_sutra_ocean_jainism_en-blcr.228)). The passage also mentions "eighty-three days in a state inferior to perfection," ([Kalpa Sūtra](https://oceanlibrary.com/kalpa-sutra/?paraId=para_175&selectionString=kalpa_sutra_ocean_jainism_en-blcr.0~kalpa_sutra_ocean_jainism_en-blcr.228)) a detail the summary of his life does not have to hold, and one worth noticing.

**The serpent and the ascetic.** Buehler summarises the Jaina Purāṇas. Two brothers, Marubhūti and Kamaṭha, were enemies through eight successive lives and were reborn as Pārśvanātha and Sambaradeva. A brahmin performing the *pañcāgni* rite felled a tree that held two snakes; Pārśva protested, and the snakes, cut in pieces, were restored to life and reborn as Dharaṇendra and Padmāvatī. Later Sambaradeva, also called Meghakumāra, attacked Pārśva with a storm while he stood motionless in meditation, and then, Buehler writes, "Dharaṇendra spread his many hoods over the head of the Arhata," while Padmāvatī held a white umbrella over him ([Buehler, *On the Indian Sect of the Jainas*](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11897)). Buehler also compares the scene to Māra's attack on the Buddha at Bodh-gayā. I read this as the reason the serpent-king's hood appears in his images: it is the sign of that protection.

**The four vows.** Pārśva is associated with four vows, where Mahāvīra's community kept five. The [*Uttarādhyayana*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21347) commentary explains that chastity "is not explicitly mentioned among Pârsva's four vows" but was understood to be included in them ([*Uttarādhyayana*](https://oceanlibrary.com/uttaradhyayana/?paraId=fn_273)). Buehler reports that the Jaina works give an "oft repeated assertion" that resolves the difference ([Buehler, *On the Indian Sect of the Jainas*](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11897)). Hermann Jacobi, translating the *Uttarādhyayana*, notes that the Pāli term *cātuyāma* corresponds to the Prākrit term for Pārśva's four vows, and he suggests the Buddhists may have attributed the doctrine to Mahāvīra by mistake ([Jacobi, *Uttarādhyayana*](https://oceanlibrary.com/uttaradhyayana)).

**What these sources do not settle.** The passages I found do not give the Digambara version of the Marubhūti–Kamaṭha story, which Buehler only summarises, and they do not describe Pārśva's death or the hill tradition connected with him. Pārśva is traditionally associated with Sammeta (Pārśvanātha) hill as the place of his liberation, but these passages do not confirm that.

The thread I would pull is the *Kalpa Sūtra*'s full account of his life, which the passage above only opens, together with the Digambara telling of the brothers' story. Both would show you how the Jain narrative holds the serpent, the ascetic and the storm together.

With warm wishes,
Anís

gemini-3.1-flash-lite.reply:
It is a pleasure to explore the figure of Pārśvanātha with you. In the narrative tradition of the Jainas, he stands as the twenty-third *tīrthaṅkara*—a "ford-maker" who has crossed the ocean of existence and established the path for others to follow.

**Identity and Iconography**
Pārśvanātha is distinguished in Jain iconography by the presence of snake-hoods sheltering his head. As noted by Johann Georg Buehler, while the images of the *tīrthaṅkaras* are generally uniform—seated in meditation with legs crossed and hands resting in the lap—Pārśvanātha is the one consistently marked by the serpent symbol ([On the Indian Sect of the Jainas](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11897)). His traditional attributes include a blue color, the *dhātakī* tree, and his constant attendants, the *yakṣa* Dharaṇendra and the *yakṣiṇī* Padmāvatī ([On the Indian Sect of the Jainas](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11897)).

**The Legend of Protection**
The serpent-hoods are not merely symbolic; they are rooted in a narrative of protection. The *Jaina Purāṇas* recount that Pārśvanātha and his antagonist, Sambaradeva (born from the enmity of two brothers, Marubhūti and Kamaṭha, through eight incarnations), crossed paths when Pārśvanātha intervened to save two snakes from a ritual fire ([On the Indian Sect of the Jainas](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11897)). These snakes were reborn as the divine beings Dharaṇendra and Padmāvatī. Later, when Sambaradeva attacked the meditating Pārśvanātha with a great storm, Dharaṇendra shielded him:

> "Dharaṇendra spread his many hoods over the head of the Arhata and the Yakshṅî Padmāvatî held a white umbrella (_śveta chhatri_) over him for protection. Ever after they became his constant attendants" ([On the Indian Sect of the Jainas](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11897)).

**Lifespan and Historical Context**
The [*Kalpa Sūtra*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21345) provides a specific account of his life, detailing his transition from a householder to an ascetic:

> "In that period, in that age the Arhat Pâr_s_va, the people’s favourite, lived thirty years as a householder, eighty-three days in a state inferior to perfection, something less than seventy years as a Kevalin, full seventy years as a _S_rama_n_a, and a hundred years on the whole" ([Kalpa Sūtra](https://oceanlibrary.com/kalpa-sutra/?paraId=para_175&selectionString=kalpa_sutra_ocean_jainism_en-blcr.0~kalpa_sutra_ocean_jainism_en-blcr.228)).

**The Four Vows**
A significant distinction in the Jain tradition is the evolution of the monastic vows. Pārśvanātha is said to have taught four vows (*caturyāma*), while Mahāvīra, the twenty-fourth *tīrthaṅkara*, added the fifth ([On the Indian Sect of the Jainas](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11897)). Scholars like Hermann Jacobi and the [*Uttaradhyayana*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21347) suggest that the fifth vow—chastity—was implicit in the original four, though it became necessary to make it explicit as the moral discipline of the order shifted over time ([Uttaradhyayana](https://oceanlibrary.com/uttaradhyayana/?paraId=fn_273)) ([Uttaradhyayana](https://oceanlibrary.com/uttaradhyayana)).

To see how the original language of the *caturyāma* is framed, we can look at how the term appears in the context of the Buddhist texts, which often refer to the Nigaṇṭha (Jain) creed:

```bilingual
the Pâli kâtuyâma is equivalent to the Prâkṛit kâtuggâma <sup>1</sup>
the Pâli kâtuyâma is equivalent to the Prâkṛit kâtuggâma <sup>2</sup>
a well-known Gaina term which denotes the four vows of Pârsva <sup>3</sup>
a well-known Gaina term which denotes the four vows of Pârsva <sup>4</sup>
in contradistinction to the five vows of Mahâvîra <sup>5</sup>
in contradistinction to the five vows of Mahâvîra <sup>6</sup>
```
<sup>1</sup> *Uttaradhyayana*, tr. Hermann Jacobi · <sup>2</sup> *Uttaradhyayana*, tr. Hermann Jacobi · <sup>3</sup> *Uttaradhyayana*, tr. Hermann Jacobi · <sup>4</sup> *Uttaradhyayana*, tr. Hermann Jacobi · <sup>5</sup> *Uttaradhyayana*, tr. Hermann Jacobi · <sup>6</sup> *Uttaradhyayana*, tr. Hermann Jacobi

It is worth noting that while these sources provide a clear narrative and historical framework, they are scholarly and canonical summaries rather than modern doctrinal commentaries. The library does not contain specific primary texts detailing his final days on Sammeta hill, though that remains a central part of the tradition's geography.

If you find yourself drawn further into these narratives, you might look into the *Kalpa Sūtra* for the fuller biographical account of his life, or perhaps explore the Digambara versions of the Marubhūti–Kamaṭha cycle, which offer a more expansive view of the karmic entanglement between the two figures.

gemini-3.5-flash-lite.reply:
Hello! Pārśvanātha, the twenty-third ford-maker (*tīrthaṅkara*) of the Jain tradition, is known through narrative and legendary accounts preserved in both canonical literature and early scholarly studies of Jainism.

**Identity and Iconography**
In the traditional series of Jinas, Pārśvanātha stands as the twenty-third, immediately preceding Mahāvīra [1, 7, 41]. Johann Georg Buehler's study of the Jainas records his standard iconographic markers: a blue complexion, a serpent emblem, a lifespan of a hundred years, the *dhātakī* tree, and his attending *yakṣa* (Pārśva or Dharaṇendra) and *yakṣiṇī* (Padmāvatī) ([On the Indian Sect of the Jainas](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11897)). Visually, his images are distinguished from those of other Tīrthakaras by the serpent-hoods spread over his head ([On the Indian Sect of the Jainas](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11897)). While Digambara and Śvetāmbara images differ in whether they are depicted nude or clothed, Pārśvanātha's snake-hoods remain a defining feature in both traditions ([On the Indian Sect of the Jainas](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11897)).

**Lifespan**
The [*Kalpa Sūtra*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=21345) records that Pārśvanātha lived a total of one hundred years: thirty years as a householder, a period in a state inferior to perfection, a little under seventy years as a *Kevalin* (an omniscient being), and seventy years in total as a *Śramaṇa* (an ascetic) ([Kalpa Sūtra](https://oceanlibrary.com/kalpa-sutra/?paraId=para_175&selectionString=kalpa_sutra_ocean_jainism_en-blcr.0~kalpa_sutra_ocean_jainism_en-blcr.228)).

**The Serpent Legend**
A prominent cycle of legends, summarised by Buehler from the Jaina *Purāṇas*, connects Pārśvanātha with the serpent-king Dharaṇendra through successive births ([On the Indian Sect of the Jainas](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11897)). The narrative tells of two brothers, Marubhūti and Kamaṭha, who were enemies across eight incarnations and were finally reborn as Pārśvanātha and Sambaradeva ([On the Indian Sect of the Jainas](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11897)). When an unbeliever performing a five-fire (*pañcāgni*) rite felled a tree containing two snakes despite Pārśva's remonstrance, the snakes were cut into pieces ([On the Indian Sect of the Jainas](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11897)). Pārśva restored them to life using the *pañcamantra*, and they were subsequently reborn in the underworld as Dharaṇendra and Padmāvatī ([On the Indian Sect of the Jainas](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11897)).

Later, when Sambaradeva attacked Pārśva with a violent storm while the Jina stood motionless in deep meditation (*kâyotsarga*), Dharaṇendra's throne shook ([On the Indian Sect of the Jainas](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11897)). The serpent-king and his consort sped to protect their former benefactor, with Dharaṇendra spreading his manifold serpent-hoods over Pārśva's head while Padmāvatī held a white umbrella (*śveta chhatri*) above him ([On the Indian Sect of the Jainas](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11897)). This legend explains the origin of the serpent canopy that shelters his images [3, 7].

**The Four Vows**
Jain texts frequently address an apparent discrepancy regarding Pārśvanātha's ethical discipline, noting that he taught four vows (*caturyāma*) rather than the five (*pañca mahāvratas*) taught by Mahāvīra ([On the Indian Sect of the Jainas](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/11897)). As Hermann Jacobi and canonical commentaries explain, the vow of chastity was not explicitly enumerated among Pārśva's four vows because it was understood to be implicitly enjoined within them [4, 5]. Buddhist texts also reference this earlier fourfold teaching (*cātuyāma*), which scholars view as an echo of Pārśva's historical precedence before Mahāvīra added the fifth vow ([Uttaradhyayana](https://oceanlibrary.com/uttaradhyayana)).

It is worth noting that while traditional accounts connect Pārśva's final liberation to Sammeta (Pārśvanātha) hill—the primary Jain pilgrimage site—the sources retrieved in this search do not elaborate on that event, focusing instead on his iconography, lifespan, legends, and teachings as recorded by early scholars and the *Kalpa Sūtra* [1, 2, 3, 6].

Would you like to explore the full account of Pārśva's life as preserved in the *Kalpa Sūtra*?

base.reply:
Dear friend,

The five books of the Torah don't name Jesus or tell of his death. What the Bahá'í texts offer is 'Abdu'l-Bahá's reading of the Torah's promises of a Messiah, and of how those who awaited him came to crucify him.

**The signs, read literally.** 'Abdu'l-Bahá describes a people praying daily for the Messiah's coming. They reasoned that ["The Revelation of Christ, according to the clear text of the Torah, will be attested by certain signs"](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-abdul-baha), and that anyone claiming it without them was an impostor. The signs they listed included that ["the Messiah should come from an unknown place"](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-abdul-baha), whereas they knew the man's house in Nazareth. Another was that ["He shall rule with a rod of iron"](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-abdul-baha), while this Messiah had not even a wooden staff. A third was sitting on David's throne, and a fourth was upholding all the laws of the Torah. He concludes that, because they did not grasp these signs, ["they crucified the Word of God"](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-abdul-baha/?paraId=para_182&selectionString=selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_8c.0~selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_8c.669).

**The signs, read spiritually.**

> Now the Bahá’ís hold that the recorded signs did come to pass in the Manifestation of Christ, although not in the sense which the Jews understood, the description in the Torah being allegorical.
>
> — 'Abdu'l-Bahá, [*Selections from the Writings of 'Abdu'l-Bahá*](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-abdul-baha/?paraId=para_182&selectionString=selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_8c.0~selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_8c.669)

His example is sovereignty. Christ's was heavenly and everlasting, ["not a Napoleonic sovereignty that vanisheth in a short time"](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-abdul-baha/?paraId=para_182&selectionString=selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_8c.0~selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_8c.669), and it has endured nearly two thousand years. He adds that ["all the other signs have been made manifest, but the Jews did not understand"](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-abdul-baha/?paraId=para_183&selectionString=selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_8d.0~selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_8d.243).

**Daniel's seventy weeks.** The most direct link to the death itself is in [*Some Answered Questions*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20911). Daniel (which I'd note sits in the wider Hebrew Scriptures rather than the five books) fixes a period ending in the martyrdom of Christ, ["for it is through the martyrdom of Christ that the sacrifice is ended and the altar destroyed"](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_149&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_76.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_76.218). 'Abdu'l-Bahá counts from the edict issued in 457 B.C. Seventy weeks is 490 days, and a day is a year, since the Torah says ["The day of the Lord is one year"](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_151&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_78.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_78.419). Since ["Christ was thirty-three years old at the time of His martyrdom and ascension"](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_151&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_78.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_78.419), 457 plus 33 gives the 490.

**Foreknowledge isn't cause.** If the prophets foretold the death, did their words bring it about? 'Abdu'l-Bahá answers that the Prophets learned through revelation that Christ would be martyred, and that ["This knowledge is a sign of their perfection and not the cause of His martyrdom"](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_494&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_gq.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_gq.396).

A word on scope. I found no passage here where the Bahá'í texts take up the specific verses Christians often cite, such as Isaiah 53 or Psalm 22, so I won't put words in their mouth about those. The calendar reading of Daniel and the allegorical reading of the messianic signs are what 'Abdu'l-Bahá himself sets out.

If you'd like to go further, the chapters of *Some Answered Questions* around the Daniel prophecy are worth reading whole. There he sets the arithmetic inside a larger question: what does it mean for a promise to be fulfilled, and by what kind of kingdom?

With warm wishes,
Anís

claude-haiku-5-5.reply:
Dear friend,

The passages I found don't contain the Torah's own words about Jesus' death. They contain 'Abdu'l-Bahá's reading of how the Torah's promises of the Messiah relate to Christ's death. As background of my own, the Five Books do not name Jesus or describe his crucifixion. That comes from general knowledge, not from these passages.

**The promise, and the Jews' reading of it.** 'Abdu'l-Bahá says the Torah did promise the One who came, and that the Jews did not grasp what its signs meant: "as they did not understand the meaning of these signs, they crucified the Word of God" ([*Selections from the Writings of 'Abdu'l-Bahá*](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-abdul-baha/?paraId=para_182&selectionString=selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_8c.0~selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_8c.669)).

His account of their objections is concrete. They expected the Messiah to come from a known place, to rule "with a rod of iron," ([Selections from the Writings of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-abdul-baha)) and to sit on David's throne. Of the last, he has them say that this man "has not even a mat to sit on" ([*Selections from the Writings of 'Abdu'l-Bahá*](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-abdul-baha)). Because these signs were not seen in the form they expected, they called him an impostor.

**Fulfilled, but not in the literal sense.** This is the centre of his answer. The signs, he says, "did come to pass in the Manifestation of Christ, although not in the sense which the Jews understood, the description in the Torah being allegorical" ([*Selections from the Writings of 'Abdu'l-Bahá*](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-abdul-baha/?paraId=para_182&selectionString=selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_8c.0~selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_8c.669)). He takes sovereignty as his example:

> For Bahá'ís say that the sovereignty of Christ was a heavenly, divine, everlasting sovereignty, not a Napoleonic sovereignty that vanisheth in a short time. — [*Selections from the Writings of 'Abdu'l-Bahá*](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-abdul-baha/?paraId=para_182&selectionString=selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_8c.0~selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_8c.669)

He adds that "all the other signs have been made manifest, but the Jews did not understand" ([*Selections from the Writings of 'Abdu'l-Bahá*](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-abdul-baha/?paraId=para_183&selectionString=selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_8d.0~selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_8d.243)).

**Foreknowledge did not cause the death.** A reader might ask whether the prophets' knowledge made the crucifixion happen. 'Abdu'l-Bahá says the prophets "came to know that Christ would be martyred, which they in turn proclaimed," and then answers directly: "This knowledge is a sign of their perfection and not the cause of His martyrdom" ([*Some Answered Questions*](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_494&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_gq.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_gq.396)).

**Daniel's seventy weeks.** Here he reads a prophecy as pointing to Christ's death. The Book of Daniel "fixes the period between the rebuilding of Jerusalem and the martyrdom of Christ," because "it is through the martyrdom of Christ that the sacrifice is ended and the altar destroyed" ([*Some Answered Questions*](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_149&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_76.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_76.218)). His arithmetic relies on the Torah's principle that "the day of the Lord is one year." ([Some Answered Questions](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_151&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_78.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_78.419)) He takes seventy weeks as 490 years, counting from the edict issued in 457 B.C. and adding Christ's age of thirty-three at his death: "Thirty-three added to 457 is 490" ([*Some Answered Questions*](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_151&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_78.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_78.419)).

**How to hold this.** The Torah text itself is not in these passages. What they give is 'Abdu'l-Bahá's authorized exposition of its promises. The Daniel calculation is his, and so is the claim that the signs are allegorical. My own reading is that he is less concerned with proving the death than with explaining why its meaning was missed. That reading is mine, not his.

If you want to follow the thread, begin with the Daniel chapters of [*Some Answered Questions*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20911). Then look for the chapter on the "two Manifestations," where he connects the Torah's promises to Christ and to the Báb and Bahá'u'lláh. I would be curious what you make of the sovereignty example when you read it in context.

With warmth,
Anís

gemini-3.1-flash-lite.reply:
Hello. It is a pleasure to explore this with you.

The Torah, as the Five Books of Moses, does not name Jesus or explicitly describe his death. Instead, the Bahá’í Writings treat the Torah as a collection of prophecies and signs that set the stage for the coming of the Messiah. From this perspective, the Torah’s silence on the specific event of the crucifixion is not a lack of relevance, but rather a reflection of how the Jewish people of that time interpreted their own scriptures.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains that the Jews expected the Messiah to appear in a way that aligned with a literal reading of the Torah. Because they looked for signs such as the Messiah coming from an unknown place, ruling with a "rod of iron," or physically sitting on the throne of David, they did not recognize Jesus when he appeared. As ‘Abdu’l-Bahá notes:

> "But as they did not understand the meaning of these signs, they crucified the Word of God. Now the Bahá’ís hold that the recorded signs did come to pass in the Manifestation of Christ, although not in the sense which the Jews understood, the description in the Torah being allegorical." [1](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-abdul-baha/?paraId=para_182&selectionString=selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_8c.0~selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_8c.669)

In this view, the "signs" were fulfilled, but they were spiritual rather than material. For instance, the sovereignty promised to the Messiah was not a political or military power, but a "heavenly, divine, everlasting sovereignty" that has endured for two millennia [3](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-abdul-baha/?paraId=para_182&selectionString=selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_8c.0~selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_8c.669).

While the Torah does not detail the crucifixion, the Writings look to the Book of Daniel to provide a prophetic timeline that includes it. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá interprets the "seventy weeks" in Daniel as a period of 490 years, using the principle that "the day of the Lord is one year." ([Some Answered Questions](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_151&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_78.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_78.419)) By calculating from the third edict of Artaxerxes in 457 B.C., he arrives at the time of Christ’s life and death:

> "The Book of Daniel fixes the period between the rebuilding of Jerusalem and the martyrdom of Christ at seventy weeks, for it is through the martyrdom of Christ that the sacrifice is ended and the altar destroyed. This prophecy thus refers to the advent of Christ." [6](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_149&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_76.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_76.218)

It is also important to note that the prophets’ foreknowledge of this event was not the cause of it. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá clarifies that when the prophets spoke of the martyrdom of Christ, they were demonstrating their spiritual insight, not dictating the actions of those who opposed him [5](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_494&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_gq.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_gq.396).

While many traditions look to passages like Isaiah 53 as a direct prophecy of the crucifixion, the Bahá’í Writings do not expound upon that specific text in this context. The focus remains on the broader principle that the Torah’s promises were fulfilled in the person of Christ, even when the literal expectations of the time were not met.

If you are interested in how these prophetic timelines are applied to other figures, you might find it rewarding to look at the chapters in [*Some Answered Questions*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20911) where ‘Abdu’l-Bahá discusses the "two Manifestations" and the fulfillment of the Daniel prophecy in the context of the Báb and Bahá’u’lláh.

Warmly,

Anís

Hello!

The Torah (the Five Books) does not actually name Jesus or describe his death. Instead, the Bahá'í texts look to the Torah's messianic promises as the background against which Christ's life and crucifixion are understood.

As 'Abdu'l-Bahá explains, the Jewish people awaited the Messiah according to a literal reading of the Torah's signs—expecting him to emerge from an unknown place, rule with an iron rod, sit on the earthly throne of David, and uphold the outward laws of the Torah without abrogation (as recorded in [*Selections from the Writings of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20910)). Because Jesus did not fit these literal expectations, they rejected him and, as ‘Abdu'l-Bahá states, ["crucified the Word of God" ([Selections from the Writings of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-abdul-baha/?paraId=para_182&selectionString=selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_8c.0~selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_8c.669))](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-abdul-baha/?paraId=para_182&selectionString=selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdul_baha_en_8c.0~selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdul_baha_en_8c.669) - *Selections from the Writings of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá*.

The Bahá'í teachings hold that these Torah descriptions were allegorical rather than literal. The signs did come to pass, but in a spiritual sense: Christ's sovereignty, for instance, was ["a heavenly, divine, everlasting sovereignty, not a Napoleonic sovereignty that vanisheth in a short time" ([Selections from the Writings of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-abdul-baha/?paraId=para_182&selectionString=selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_8c.0~selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdu_l_baha_en_8c.669))](https://oceanlibrary.com/selections-from-the-writings-of-abdul-baha/?paraId=para_182&selectionString=selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdul_baha_en_8c.0~selections_from_the_writings_of_the_abdul_baha_en_8c.669) (*Selections from the Writings of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá*).

Similarly, the Writings connect the Torah's temporal calculations to the events of Christ's life. In [*Some Answered Questions*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20911), ‘Abdu’l-Bahá examines the "seventy weeks" prophecy in the Book of Daniel, calculating 490 years from the third edict of Artaxerxes in 457 B.C.—using the biblical principle that a day stands for a year—to arrive at the time of [“the martyrdom of Christ”](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_149&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_76.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_76.218) at age thirty-three (*Some Answered Questions*).

As for the prophets foreseeing this suffering, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá notes that foreknowledge did not cause the event; rather, knowing beforehand that Christ would be martyred [“is a sign of their perfection and not the cause of His martyrdom”](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha/?paraId=para_494&selectionString=some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_gq.0~some-answered-questions-prod-version_en_gq.396) (*Some Answered Questions*).

If you would like to explore this further, you might enjoy reading more of *Some Answered Questions*, particularly the chapters where ‘Abdu’l-Bahá discusses biblical prophecies and the fulfillment of past scriptures.

Warmly,
Anís

base.reply:
Dear friend,

You're right about the fragment. In [*Sutra Collection (S)*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20937) the lines read: ["If non-attachment did exist, it couldn't be described as a negation. The absence of attributes indicates negation."](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-s/?paraId=para_105&selectionString=sutracollection_s_ocean_buddhism_en-bl6t.0~sutracollection_s_ocean_buddhism_en-bl6t.194) The passage goes on: "Anything not negated has attributes. Anything with attributes exists. How could that define non-attachment?" That is one move in an argument, and it ends in a challenge rather than a definition. It gives me no sutra number, and the library's label gives the translator only as "Unknown." My earlier remark that Buddhist texts "deconstruct clinging itself" went further than this fragment can carry, and I'd set it aside.

There are passages where the Buddha speaks of dispassion (virāga) in his own voice and the sutta is named. None is a formal definition. Each shows what dispassion does.

**MN 147, the Cula-Rahulovada Sutta**, in Thanissaro Bhikkhu's translation, is the clearest:

> "He grows disenchanted with the intellect, disenchanted with ideas, disenchanted with consciousness at the intellect, disenchanted with contact at the intellect. … Disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is fully released."
> — [Majjhima Nikaya 147 - Cula-Rahulovada Sutta: The Shorter Exposition to Rahula](https://oceanlibrary.com/dhammapada_buddha)

— [*Majjhima Nikaya 147*](https://oceanlibrary.com/dhammapada_buddha)

Dispassion here is the middle step: disenchantment, then dispassion, then release. It comes from seeing clearly, and it leads to freedom.

**SN 54.9, the Vesali Sutta**, also in Thanissaro's translation, places it in practice. The monk trains: ["I will breathe in focusing on dispassion [literally, fading]."](https://oceanlibrary.com/dhammapada_buddha) It comes in a sequence with inconstancy, cessation and relinquishment. Thanissaro's gloss "literally, fading" suggests something that gradually loosens rather than something forced.

**Sutra Collection (M, Part-2)** shows dispassion at the goal. Of Unbinding the Buddha says the one who knows it does not conceive it as "mine" and does not delight in it: ["Because, with the ending of passion, he is devoid of passion, I tell you."](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-m-part-2/?paraId=para_1399&selectionString=sutra_collection_m_part_2_ocean_buddhism_en-bl17c.0~sutra_collection_m_part_2_ocean_buddhism_en-bl17c.316) I can quote those words, but the library gives no sutta number for them, and I can't supply one from here.

So the sources here show dispassion as a fading of passion that follows disenchantment and opens into release. The sutta names for the first two I can give with confidence. For the two lines in the Sutra Collection, the location isn't established here. It would have to come from a Pali edition or a translation that carries sutta numbers.

A thread you might pull: look at how the Pali words virāga and vīta-rāga (literally "fading of passion" and "gone-passion") are used around MN 147 and SN 54.9. The same root appears in both.

With warm regards,
Anís

claude-haiku-5-5.reply:
Not a formal definition, as far as I found. The closest passages show the Buddha teaching dispassion as a step in a sequence, and as an object of breath meditation.

**Cūḷa-Rāhulovāda Sutta (MN 147)**: In [*Majjhima Nikaya 147*](https://siftersearch.com/library/buddhist/pali-canon/tr-thanissaro_majjhima-nikaya-140-dhatuvibhanga-sutta-analysis-of-properties), the Cula-Rahulovada Sutta, in Thanissaro Bhikkhu's translation, the teaching runs in order: ["Disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is fully released."](https://oceanlibrary.com/dhammapada_buddha) Dispassion comes after disenchantment and before release. The passage shows what dispassion leads to, but it does not say what dispassion is in itself.

**Saṃyutta Nikāya 54.9 (Vesālī Sutta)**: In [*Samyutta Nikaya 54.9*](https://siftersearch.com/library/buddhist/pali-canon/tr-thanissaro_samyutta-nikaya-54-8-dipa-sutta-the-lamp), the Vesali Sutta, also in Thanissaro's translation, the Buddha trains a practitioner in breathing: ["He trains himself, 'I will breathe in focusing on dispassion"](https://oceanlibrary.com/dhammapada_buddha), with the translator's gloss "literally, fading." Here dispassion is something the mind is trained to focus on. The word behind "dispassion" is virāga. Its literal sense is a fading away or loosening of passion, which fits the translator's gloss.

**Sutra Collection (M, Part-2)**: The library gives the translator as "Unknown" and no sutra number. The passage says of Unbinding: ["Because, with the ending of passion, he is devoid of passion, I tell you."](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-m-part-2/?paraId=para_1399&selectionString=sutra_collection_m_part_2_ocean_buddhism_en-bl17c.0~sutra_collection_m_part_2_ocean_buddhism_en-bl17c.316) This links dispassion to the goal. It does not define it.

**Sutra Collection (S)**: The line you asked about reads: ["If non-attachment did exist, it couldn't be described as a negation."](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-s/?paraId=para_105&selectionString=sutracollection_s_ocean_buddhism_en-bl6t.0~sutracollection_s_ocean_buddhism_en-bl6t.194) The surrounding lines argue about whether non-attachment can be defined by negation. The text I have does not show who is speaking, and it has no sutra name or number, so I can't place it. My earlier reading, that Buddhist texts "deconstruct clinging itself," rested on this fragment and goes further than it supports. I withdraw it.

So I didn't find a passage where the Buddha defines virāga or non-attachment in those words, with a sutta number. The two Thanissaro passages are the ones to hold onto, because they show dispassion at work in the teaching with their numbers attached.

The thread to pull is the Pali itself. Find MN 147 and SN 54.9 in an edition that gives sutta numbers, and look at how virāga appears in each place. Then compare the translator's choices of "dispassion" and "fading" with the Pali words around them.

gemini-3.1-flash-lite.reply:
Dear friend,

You are quite right to press for clarity. I was mistaken to lean on that fragment from the [*Sutra Collection (S)*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20937) as a definition of non-attachment; it is, as you noted, a rhetorical question posed within a debate, and it does not represent the Buddha’s own account of the practice. I appreciate you holding me to the text—it is a good reminder to look for the Buddha’s own voice rather than fragments of argument.

The library does not contain a formal, dictionary-style definition of "non-attachment" or *virāga* (dispassion). Instead, the Buddha describes it as a process or a sequence of mental states. The clearest instance of this is in the *Cula-Rahulovada Sutta* (MN 147), where he outlines how one moves from disenchantment to release:

> "He grows disenchanted with the intellect, disenchanted with ideas, disenchanted with consciousness at the intellect, disenchanted with contact at the intellect. And whatever there is that arises in dependence on contact at the intellect as a mode of feeling, a mode of perception, a mode of fabrication, or a mode of consciousness: With that, too, he grows disenchanted. Disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is fully released. With full release, there is the knowledge, 'Fully released.'" [1](https://oceanlibrary.com/dhammapada_buddha)

Here, *virāga* (dispassion) is not a static concept but a vital step in a chain of events. It is the bridge between seeing the nature of things and being "fully released."

In the *Vesali Sutta* (SN 54.9), the Buddha places this same concept directly into the practice of meditation, showing it as a focus of the mind:

> "He trains himself, 'I will breathe in focusing on dispassion [literally, fading].' He trains himself, 'I will breathe out focusing on dispassion.'" [2](https://oceanlibrary.com/dhammapada_buddha)

In this context, *virāga* is a way of training the mind to observe the "fading" of things, rather than a doctrine to be held. Similarly, in the [*Sutra Collection (M, Part-2)*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20937), the Buddha links dispassion to the state of the practitioner:

> “Why is that? Because, with the ending of passion, he is devoid of passion, I tell you.” [3](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-m-part-2/?paraId=para_1399&selectionString=sutra_collection_m_part_2_ocean_buddhism_en-bl17c.0~sutra_collection_m_part_2_ocean_buddhism_en-bl17c.316)

While these passages show how the Buddha uses the term, they do not offer a single, definitive "what is" statement. My earlier suggestion that the texts "deconstruct clinging itself" was my own synthesis, and it went beyond what these passages actually state.

If you would like to explore this further, you might look at the Pali terms *virāga* (dispassion) and *vīta-rāga* (devoid of passion) in an edition that provides the original text alongside the translation. Seeing the original language in the context of these specific sutta numbers could help you see how the Buddha’s usage holds together across different teachings.

Warmly,

Anís

My earlier reading of Buddhist texts as "deconstructing clinging itself" was built upon a fragment—the line «The absence of attributes indicates negation» ([*Sutra Collection (S)*](https://siftersearch.com/library/view?doc=20937) ([Sutra Collection (S)](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-s/?paraId=para_105&selectionString=sutracollection_s_ocean_buddhism_en-bl6t.0~sutracollection_s_ocean_buddhism_en-bl6t.194)))—that sits within a debate rather than offering the Buddha's own account, and it goes well beyond what that passage actually supports. [literally,
fading].' He trains himself, 'I will breathe out focusing on dispassion.' [15] He trains himself, 'I will breathe in focusing on cessation.' He trains h"](https://oceanlibrary.com/dhammapada_buddha) — *Samyutta Nikaya 54.9 - Vesali Sutta* ([Samyutta Nikaya 54.9 - Vesali Sutta: At Vesali](https://oceanlibrary.com/dhammapada_buddha))

In the *Sutra Collection (M, Part-2)* ([Sutra Collection (M, Part-2)](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-m-part-2/?paraId=para_1399&selectionString=sutra_collection_m_part_2_ocean_buddhism_en-bl17c.0~sutra_collection_m_part_2_ocean_buddhism_en-bl17c.316)), the text approaches the goal of Unbinding (*Nibbana*) by showing how a practitioner relates to it once passion has ended:

> ["He directly knows Unbinding as Unbinding. Directly knowing Unbinding as Unbinding, he does not conceive things about Unbinding, does not conceive things in Unbinding, does not conceive things coming out of Unbinding, does not conceive Unbinding as ‘mine,’ does not delight in Unbinding. Why is that? Because, with the ending of passion, he is devoid of passion, I tell you."](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-m-part-2/?paraId=para_1399&selectionString=sutra_collection_m_part_2_ocean_buddhism_en-bl17c.0~sutra_collection_m_part_2_ocean_buddhism_en-bl17c.316) — *Sutra Collection (M, Part-2)* ([Sutra Collection (M, Part-2)](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-m-part-2/?paraId=para_1399&selectionString=sutra_collection_m_part_2_ocean_buddhism_en-bl17c.0~sutra_collection_m_part_2_ocean_buddhism_en-bl17c.316))

These passages suggest that rather than offering a static definition, the texts present *virāga* as a lived movement of the mind—a fading of passion that arises through clear seeing and practical meditation, culminating in release.

Warmly,
